div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MT DEAR NELLIE,

The recent spring-like weather has made every- one's winter hats and toques look rather shabby; but it is yet too early to be buying one's Millinery for the height of the season. Yet there are a number of excellent fashions about. A friend of mine has a toque of coarse black straw, in a new and quaint shape, trimmed with quills and large clusters of roses and foliage, in any colour, on the left side. Another charming hat lu-A a trans- parent crown of creamy guipure lace, and a brim of white tulle, veiled with black sequin horsehair net. On the left side there was a high white osprey, and a wreath of pink roses and foliage. Yet another straw hat is trimmed with palest blush roses, and has a few folds of pastel blue velvet under the brim at the left side and it certainly is delightfully scoming to fresh and dainty faces. A tall wir.e bow of black velvet ribbon gives value to the .'•ues in the flowers and velvet.

For outdoor garm az.z.s vague tones of grey are in fashion. Elephant, mouse and kindred tints seem to assort with the excited, troubled feelings of the nation. Khaki does not differ essentially from the tan colour that has long been fashionable, but the military air imparted to materials of this colour proves how well in the foreground of our minds is our British Army in Africa. Braiding, frogs and aiguilettes, are all applied in regimental styles, and the cblue serges are being braided hi black to meet the general desire to have some. thing in affinity with the war. Braid manufac- turers should be busy. On one coat and skirt alone there are fifteen yards of wide military braid and thirty of the narrow, tubular sort.

A little coat which I had shown to me recently is velvet, embroidered with silk braid and jet. The back is very slightly cut up in the centre, the two sides being rounded off at the edges. The revers are in black satin, the design being appliqué in grey panne, veined with steel beads. A very pretty yet useful little cloth coat seen the other day had revers and collar of deep yet vivid rose red corded silk, edged with a black and white galon. The coat was lined with rose-colour, &e was the skirt of the same cloth, this latter being pleated and stitched from waist to knee in the most approved fashion of to-day. Accompanied by a toque of black straw and tulle, with a bunch of shaded red carnations under the brim, the effect of the whole was excellent. A few white cloth coats, slightly toned down with black trimmings, are seen, but they are too conspicuous to be very favourably regarded by women of really good taste. The same remarks apply equally to the pale grey coats—silk or cloth—covered with cream guipure, which are being shown by so many fashionable modistes.

A ,ilend has bee... showing me a neat walking dress made of lieze, with one of the new bolero bodices. The c tour of the frieze is a clear, cold grey, with a litt )mixture of sea-blue, forest-green, and soft amber. The skirt opens at the side, hav- ing no opening at the back. At the neck and at the top of the arm ; there is pleated green silk and shamrock embroid, t'y on green. The two points of the bolero fastei. with buttons matching those on the skirt.

Now the days are getting, warmer, I suppose parasols will be in request. The shops, of course, are ready for the emergency with some most attractive models, the distinctive characteristic 01 •Which is their uniformity throughout of a single colour. A turquoise-blue silk sunshine will be mounted on an enamelled frame, stick, and handle to match, the stick embraced by a bunch of ribbons precisely its shade. The purest and most infantile colours, such as pink, dove, and spring green, are in better taste than any amount of splendour and trimming; indeed, extraordinary effects are just the ones that are not to be sought for now. A light ruching of tulle, a little lace insertion, or ruffling of fringe is sufficient adornment. No need there be any hard and fast line laid down as to the sunshade matching the• toilette. Not a more alluring touch of contrast could a black dress have than a rose-pink parasol, or a white gown than one of baby blue thinks
Your loving
Jzzuriz.

div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
ff:a

BIi:FT--6. Edwards has prepared a sketch of the history of "Rule Britannia "which will no t;oubt prove interesting at this particular moment. There is by the way, every reason to telieve that tbe popular rendering of the lines "Rule Britannia! Britannia rules the waves" is erroneous,and indeed it at,psara to b.•! devoid of sense. "Rule Britannia! Britannia rule the waves" would seem to be the correct rendering. The Qesen has ever been a great lover of beauty. Her Maids of Honour are iuvariably well-favoured in this particular way, and it is no secret that should they not marry, a post, iu which they came less in contact with their Sovereign is generally found for them,so soon as the" falling off •' process commences. The great beauty of the majority • of Dublin girls is not likely theretore to be °ye:looked by the Queen. Nor are their soft musical voicee, than which few items are more ap- preciated by her Majes'y; -

_ - The birth of another sun to the Duke and Duchess of York naakee the succession in the direct lion still more secure. There is Ado cause no to anticipate that a daughter of the Duke ani Duchess of Fife will ever be called upon to reign over us. Nene rejoice over this fact more than the Duchess herself, whose one great dread tor years, was, that the crown might perchance some day fall to her lot, and her elder daughter's after her. The Princess of Wales stayed to have a peep at her new little grani'son before leaving tor Denmark where she will sped the next few weeks with her father, the King. The Duchess of York's love for pale blue is demon- strated over and over again, both at York Cottage, Sandringham, and York House, St. James's Niece. Her boudoir at York House is a truly exquisite appartnaent. The walls are panelled with damask silk, of tnis par- ticular celeur, and the three French windows are draped with ailkee hangings of the same hue, and the car set— a rich brown—is also bordered with a blue and gold patterned border which forms a very harmonious ground for the numerous sofas and chairs of white satin, and patterned Spitalfielei silks. Flowers are almost as great a necessity to the Duchess, as they are to the Princess of Wales, blooms and foliage being scattered about her apartments in richest profusion. That the white Ledge Richmond, the Duchess's old home should have passed into the hands of the Empress Frederick, is a great dis- appointment to Her Royal Highness, who had hoped, almost to the last, that this residence, much needed, would have been granted to her. 'Everyone will be glad to exchange the biting, cold winds of March, for the warmer spring weather which April should bring us. No cue has, as yet, reported the early arrival of the cuckoo, nor have we this year been favoured with any of those stories from the South which speak of early crops of strawberries, and other remark- able evidences of the forwardness of vegetation. This season everything appears to be very backward, and it is far better so, as the fruit is more likely to. escape dam- age from frost. Just now we are getting large quanti- ties of fruit from South Africa. Tee war has closed many local markets to the growers, who, as in Canada and Australia, are now giving their attention to ship- ping the produce to this country. The Colonies, with their more settled climates, escape the one great drawback to fruit culture in this country, the liability of having crops destroyed by frost, or other unfavourable conditions of the weather. Greater •care and attention is always taken in the growing of colonial ' fruit. In some parts of the Colonies, they, have a systematic method of destroying insect pests, by the, fumigation of the trees. In this country it is _quite use- less for one person to attempt to cleanse his tchard if his neighbour allows the pests to fleurieh undisturbed, and consequently nothing is done. But ill Australia they deal with the whole districts, coverinehe tree with a tent, and subjecting it to the fumes of hydrocyanic acid. Four or five men with about fifty tents will thus cover from four to six acres of orchard in a night. Once upon a time co leng as a hat pierposseseed a knob of some kind—and very often this was nothing more ornamental than a boot button—and secured one's headgear to one's head, that was all required of it. But such a state of affairs no longer obtains. The hat pin of the moment is truly a work of art, and an item of. much beauty. Real jewels are frequently employed in its manufacture, and "smart" women are careful to possess hat pins that match each set of jewellery des- tined to be worn with an outdoor costume.

1 Our bats for the coming summer promise to be very large, positive cartwheels, also very high, and that they will be worn quite on :he back of the head—halo-fashion —is now an assured fact. There is however, one saving clause in all this, these gigantic erections will be very light. Only the "airiest and fairyest" of substances are I tolerated in the millinery world such as tulle, muslin, chiffon ; gauza•ribbons; flowers made of coloured gauzes, and silk chiffon; gauze ribbons; flowers made of coloured gauzes, and silk chiffon. All the newest straws too are but a feather weight in the hand. Mr. Lone is risking Parliament for fresh powers for I dealing with dogs and dog owners, of which the chief I purport is to require all animals to wear a name and ; address collar, as a guarantee of their respectability. Dog owners are divided in opinion as to the esefulness of the measure, but the Secretary of the Canine Defence League is opposed to ito as he is apparently to any other •legislative interferenee witri he"Y friend of man." It may, however, be questioned whether the doe is not degenerating from its former hieh estate, for fashion is constantly demanding new kinds of does of purely artificial breeds,with a more or less deteriorating result to the whole canine race. To real dog-lovers, scarcely anything worse could happen to the animal, to its dignity, and self-respect,than to place it on a level with the mere capricieas whims of fashion.
" MADGE."

He tinked slyly at Ella as he said this, but she affected not to notice the remark or the meaning wink. That young Cartleigh was a flirt, or worse, was the opinion of most of the girls employed at Fernleigh Mill. He had often been seen in Oldham and Manchester in company with over- dressed females. In Dalesworth Ella Rayburn was the only girl who had "walked out" with him. He was generally considered to be a fast, wild, harum-scarum sort of fellow, but withal, not really a bad sort. It was recognised that while he had conspicuous faults, he had conspicuous virtues. The plucky rescue of Ella Rayburn, on Christmas Day was loyally put to his credit.

div.head: STEVE, THE OUTLANDER.
div.p: STEVE, THE OUTLANDER.
BY ARTHUR LAYCOCK,
Author of "The Young Gaffer," "Seaside Sketches," "Lancashire Sketches," &c.
CHAPTER XIII.

Stephen Hart wrote a lengthy epistle to his sweetheart in England, recounting in full the state of affairs in the disaffected Transvaal. He described, too, his visit to Pretoria, and being full of his new study—the Boer—wrote much concern- 'ing that interesting, but " boorish, " individual, as Ella later designated the Transvaalian. The epistle was " dry " reading to Ella. She could not grasp •aie meaning of the business. The Outlanders might be oppressed, they might have grievances, the Boers might be fools or knaves ; she could not under- stand. What she did comprehend, however, was this, that her Outlander, Steve .Hart, was not gathering much gold in the disaffected country. If the Boers were to blame for this they ought to be shot and Steve ought to be one of the shooters. He said nothing of fighting, however; he calmly talked of waiting. "Waiting, indeed!" exclaimed the disappointed girl. "As if that is a man's job, waiting for better times instead of, man-like, making the better times. Waiting, indeed! Long shall I have to wait for a home if I depend upon Steve." . • _ _

Thus she bitterly reflescted, and by such selfish thoughts was she slowly, but surely, being weaned from the former object of her regard; for affection she truly never had for anyone save herself. Of South African affairs generally she heard much from the gossiping Ben who, since Mr. Ralph had twitted him on his ignorance of matters pertaining to that country, had, by dint of arduous and prolonged study, made himself fairly well acquainted with the condition of affairs in the Transvaal.

"Yes, I know all about it," he said, as he joined Ella and her companions at breakfast-time. ".All this bother in South Afriky is caused by a lot of ign'rant, stupid, Pig-yedded Dutchmen. Boers they call 'em, an', by gow, they are bores, coo. They desarve to be bored with a two-three bullets some folks says, as that'll be th' only way lettin' a bit of sense an' civilisation into 'em; an' p'raps it would be th' handiest way. But for mysel', I'm more of a talker nor a feighter when there's lead argeyments ilyin' about. Still, summat fatal needs doin' to these Boers, for it's noan jannock 'at they should put on thoose Outlanders as is our own countrymen, yo' know, for Steve Hart is one of 'em."

"But Steve has no particular complaint to make against them," interposed Ella. "Hasn't he?" cried Ben, in well-simulated indignation. "Well, he's bin half-asleep, then, that's all I can say. If he were wideawake, same as these other lively agitatin' Outlanders, he'd be growlin' an' complainin' as a gradely English- man should do. Doesn't complain, doesn't he? Why, it's just what us Englishmen were born for, to complain an' kick up a shindy when things isn't goin' as they owt to do. It's a Englishman's birthright to growl. We're a nation of growlers. We're allus growlin' about th' weather in this country when there's nowt else to growl about, but out in South Afriky th' weather's so weel behaved, I understond, that a man, even a growlin' English- man, canno' for shame to growl at it, so what mutt he do? •Why, he mutt find summat else to growl at or else he'll not be able to keep hissel' in health. So a lot of our chaps, I tell yo' are growlin' an' grumblin' at th' Boers, an' right, too. What's th' use of havin' a British lion if it doesn't growl? Our chaps say these Boers dunnot give 'em th' franchise. Now think of that Is that fair doin's ? Is that equality, fraternity, liberty, etcettery ? Is it hek as like? Is that 'Rule Brittanyer an' Britons never sl,all be slaves' ? Is it hek as like, I say again Englishmen must have a vote, I say, though I haven't one mysel', for I got knocked off th' votin' register because I did no' pay my rates in time. How is a chap to get a cheap quart of ale if he has no vote to sell? How is a chap to uphowd th' noble British Con- stitooshun or keep his own in dacent fettle if he's no vote to fall back on? Englishmen must have a vote, lasses whether they're in scorchin' Afriky or at th' lasses, North Pow. A vote's everythin', lasses. It's like Thingummy's cocoa, it's grateful an' comfortin', even if it doesn't wash clothes. It touches th' spot in several places at once; an' though it doesn't usually fill a chap's stomach, •but oft 4 empties his yed (head), it's what every Englishman thinks a lot on. So thoose Boers had better, give th' Outlanders a vote or there'll be ructions, an' plenty of 'em." He rattled on so quickly that his hearers had no chance of slipping in a single word. "Steve must be a gradely, grumblin. growlin' • Outlander, Ella: Thee write an' tell him 'at we say so. Tell him he must uphowd th' British flag i' one hand an' .knock th' Boers down with t'other an' in an' between he must use his clogs an' punce ony o' th' t'other outlandish forriners 'at happen to be about him. You're allus safe in rincin' a forriner. They're all rascals, an' they • connot puncel yo back for they dunnot wear clogs. Tell Steve 'at if he wears his clog-toes out with his puncin' work, A I'll send him a pair o' mine at'll be the most convincin' argeyments in th' direction otth' fra.nchise 'at any man can use. I know. These clogs have bin used in many a 'lection fight. They're gradely political clogs, an' if they get 'em out in Afriky they'll win a vote for th' Outlanders, I'll be boun', in less than no time. Now yo 11 write an' tell Steve this, will yo', Ella? Tell him what we expect him to do for England, home an' beauty—meanin' yoursel'. Now yo'll tell him, won't you?" "Not I," said the girl, laughing. "I shall not tell him anything of the sort. "You-will nut; eh? Now you ought to do. You could sandwich this war-talk with your love-talk, an' they'd mix nicely. They oft go together, love an' war. Love before marriage an' war afterwards, that's th' reglar thing. I know. Well, never heed, Ella. -Just tell him to do as he likes an' he'll please us. I dunnot think, after all, that it would be a very healthy business for him to go an' fight. Ile might get killed or fatally bored hissel', an' what use :would w.vote_be to him then? He'd

better ..be wick (alive) gn' be without a vote. A live donkey's better nor a dead man. Still yo' must tell him to practise singin' Rule 13ritannyer,' an' keep his powder dry. It'll etappen keep his spirit up an' his temper down." 'Time's up, 'Ben. Yon's th' buzzer," the girls cried out as the factory whistle blew. "Yes, I hear it," said Ben, "an' time'll be up for them Boers afore long, I'm thinkin'. They'll hear a buzzer one of these fine mornings as will _make a bigger row nor this of , ours, a buzzer as will spit fire, an' death, an' desolation in th' land. Their time" be up then, mark my words." But Ben's prophecy was soon, forgotten amidst the rush and bustle of work. Pondering over her lover's letter and Ben's subsequent remarks con- cerning the unsettled state of affairs in South Africa, Ella perceived that Steve's prospects were now as bad as they possibly could be. It was very annoying, she thought. Why did he go out to such a country at such a time? Why didn't he make the best of his opportunities here? He wanted adventure, change, wanted to see life--that was his real reason for going. To make money for her was a secondary thought. He was selfish, inconsiderate, whimsical. So she assured herself, this fickle, vacillating girl of many whims. • From her lover abroad to her would-be lover at home her thoughts turned. Since Christmas Day she had not seen much of Master Ralph. He had seldom -visited the weaving-shed lately. In one of I his morning chats Ben made reference to him. I"Our young mestur," he said, "like lots of other chaps, is turnin over a new leaf this New Year, makin' good resolutions an' such things. New Tears is varry convenient for that sort o' work. Some chaps turn o'er as many new leaves in a year as would make a good-sized book, but they're blank leaves, most of 'em. New Year resolutions like pie-crusts an' lovers' promises afore marriage, are made to be broken. Never heed. If a chap makes an attempt it's summat, as Joe Batty said one fleet when he were fuddled an' tried to jump up to th' moon. If I. were Mestur Ralph I'd get wed." "Why, Ben," said' one of the listening weaver lasses, "you are always railing against wed-life." "Yee, I know; but it's nobbut my fun. If Mestur Ralph got wed his wife would reform him an' make him make resolutions that would be kept better nor his New Year's sooart, I know." "But Master Ralph's not of a marryin' sort, Ben. He believes in having many strings to his bow, and cupid's arrow doesn't seem to strike that sort." "Aye, well, many strings many troubles, many lasses many doubles. Mestur Ralph will have to have many doubles to his character if he's playin' that game. He'd be safer with one string to his bow. One lass one beau, that's a safe zoot-to. One

div.head: CHAPTER XIV,
div.p: CHAPTER XIV,

On a blustering March day Ralph Cartleigh was piloting his way along Union-street, Oldham, in the teeth of the howling gale. His hat was jammed tightly on his head, his coat buttoned plosely about his neck, and little of his face was visible. What little could be seen, however, led one to conclude that the angry spirit of the storm had entered into this stern-faced man.

Ralph Cartleigh was angry, desperately angry. This state of feeling was unusual with him, there- fore all the more remarkable. At the top of the street he turned and retraced his steps 'midst the whirl and howl Of the wind. With difficulty he held on his course, tacking to and fro like a ship labouring in a storm. Suddenly he halted as a familiar figure turned from a by- street and confronted him. _ _

"Well? " said Barrett, curtly, gripping tightly his hat, and reeling with the force of the blast. "Well, yourself," growled Ralph. "/ call it ill. Nice place this for a meeting." "Well, it's the place of meeting you proposed," snarled Barrett. "Let's go to the Beacon." "No, I'll not go there. I'm not going to have my affairs talked over there by you, who shout and bawl so that everyone can hear you." "Then come round the corner into Clegg-street. My solicitor has an office there. Perhaps that place will suit you better for our chat." Cartleigh replied with a foul oath, and the two men walked sullenly along Union-street. On the opposite side of the road a buildihg was in course of erection, and from the newly-slated roof frag- ments of slate were flying into the street below, threatening danger to passers-by. The two excited men heeded not the danger but pushed forward, talking loudly and vehemently. "I'll have it this week," said Barrett. "I'll not wait any longer. You'll pay me up or I'll-" The sentence,was cut short as, with a shriek of the hurricane, a.large 'plebe of slate swished down upon the head of the unfortunate Man, cleaving his skull. He fell to the ground senseless. A crowd soon collected, and Cartleigh assisted his com- panion into a cab whence he was conveyed to the infirmary. The ifound was serious but not of a fatal character, but would necessitate the incarcera- tion of the patient in the infirmary for many weeks. "Lucky for me," said Cartleigh, as he left the building, "but deuced unlucky for him, poor chap. 1 thought that the fates were against me, but it appears they yet smile upon me. 'Tis an ill-wind that blows nobody good, truly." He returned to Dalesworth with a lighter heart than he had set out with. Barrett had threatened to make a full exposure if his debt was not imme- diately paid. For a time, at any rate, he was foiled. Ralph reflected :that he would not be further annoyed by him for many weeks. Mean- while two hundred pounds must be raised one way or another. His father had been fairly generous of late, but refused to lend him money as formerly. Ah, his brother Henry Surely he would lend him the money. Henry, who had removed to Ancoats, Manchester, was now in receipt of a sub- stantial allowance from his father.

"He can have no particular use for the money," reflected Ralph. "He now gives it away to the poor, impoverished people of his parish. Well, I am poor and impoverished, Heaven knows, and in need of his Christian aid and ministrations. The latter he will give me willingly, I know. I must get him to give me the former. I will go to my beneficent clerical brother."

Henry Cartleigh lived in a small two-storey house in the centre of the alummiest part of unsavoury Ancoats. The dwelling was scantily furnished—a few chairs, a table, a bed, a writing- desk, and a book-case. An abode fitting to the man, one would infer, observing its quiet, unassuming, simple-living occupant. -Yet this place was a haven of rest and peace for many a tired and weary soul, a home for many a homeless Wanderer. Henry Cartleigh's interest in the slum-dwellers had first been aroused by the Ancoats Healthy Homes Society and the Ancoats Brotherhood. The good work done by these useful organisations appealed to him. He threw in his lot whole- heartedly with the kindly men and women who directed the work of the societies.

Later he decided to live amongst the slum- dwellers and know their lives as one of them. His life was hereafter given up to good works in this vile, dreary district. The poor folks about him were his constant care. He did not merely preach; he eloquently practised. Around and about him was squalor and dire misery, such as would appal and discourage most men. To Henry Cartleigh it was appalling, but his nature was not easily dis- couraged. He sought to bring a ray of sunshine and light into these dark, vile placesj and his noble efforts were in great part successful. He was devoted to his people, and they, rough, brusque, hard-drinking, hard-living fellows many of them, were equally devoted to him. • Ralph Cartleigh found his brother at home seated in the "study" (which also served as dining-room, bedroom, Ix.) perusing George's "Progress and Poverty." The slum parson rose to greet his brother and cordially shook his hand. Ralph, without any preliminary fencing, at once explained the nature of his business. "I'm a wrong un, you know, Harry. I can't help it; it's my nature, I suppose. There's no use going into explanations RS to how I've got into the pickle, and I'm not going to do it. I want two hundred pounds at once, and I must have it." "I'd give it you, Ralph, if I had it," said Henry, looking wistfully out of the window at the dingy court beyond. "I haven't the money by me now. This is a hungry place; it swallows up all my money." "Do you mean to say that you spend all your money on these filthy, drunken, good-for-nothing folks ? ,
."Not all of it, but the biggest part. I buy a few books occasionally. I bought this to-day." He held the bookup and Ralph, seeing the title, said with a cutting sneer:

. 1" Progress and Poverty,' eh? By-Jove! You need no book to shew you how to progress towards poverty. You could write one, I should think, shewing folks the nearest way, telling them to spend all their income on a lot of idle, thriftless rascals. You're a fool, Harry 1" The cleric smiled

"I mean," said Ralph, :"well, 'you're not exactly a fool bit you've as little sense as I have. We're a couple of fine fellows, brother. I get rid of my little lot pretty quick, you do the same. Mine goes to myself, yours goes to other folks. Queer that our dad should be such a grabber and we should be such spendthrifts, though you're not my sort. But, say, can't you raise the money for me somehow ? " _
"I'll get father to advance me my quarterly allowance."

"You will, Harry ? " Ralph grasped his hand and for a moment felt almost grateful to his unselfish brother. "I will, Ralph." "And I'll pay you back all right, you'll see." "When you can," said Henry. "Were it not that I shall need the money here, I would give it all to you." ' "I'll never pay him back, I'll swear ! " said Ralph to himself as he left the cottage in .grimy Ancoats. "I might as well have the rhino as these unwashed heathens."

For the next few weeks he was in good spirits. Barrett ceased from troubling and Henry forwarded his quarterly allowance in due course.• "This leaves me in quite a happy frame of mind," said Ralph. "Thanks to my simpleton of a brother I shall get out of Barrett 'E; clutches pretty soon, then I shall be able to devote my attention to one whose society is more congenial to me—sweet Ella. the charming weaver Bless me, I've not had time to think of her for months. Not .since that freezing experience at Christinas. when I do look her Up I shall male prress, rapid and sure! She won't be•as cold with me as On that delightful day-trip to Buxton. N. she'll look kindly on the erring one, now." He was not wrong in his surmise. A. few daYs later he encountered Ella Rayburn as she =IS walking through the Aelds, and her bearing towards him was most friendly. A few commonplace remarks were exchanged, then Ralph asked tho' girl if he might accompany her. yon wish," she answered,

engagingly, and togetner tney proceeaect tnrougn the green pasinres. "You like these rural walks, Miss 2.41).urn ?", the young fellow observed. - "Yes, I love the green fields. It is so pleasant to get away from the smoke to where the air is clearer and sweeter."
"It seems a pity that a pretty girl like you should be cooped up it our mill."

The girl blushed and bent her head. "Though if I had the ordering of things you wouldn't be there," he 'continued.. "Not that I would have you discharged or 'bagged 'as we call it, in the usual way. I would have you sported away to surroundings suitable to a fair being like you, to some fair, sunny spot out of sight of factories and the sound of machinery."
. - The weaver lass spoke not. She was thinking of the sunny land where Stephen Hart had hoped to make a home for her. _ _
"Cheer up, my pretty fay," said Ralph, rallyingly, .observing her depression., You mustn't lose heart because you have lost Hart." _ . .

"Mr. Cartleigh 1" cried he girl, with severity. He met her reproving glance unflinchingly. "Pardon the vile pun, Miss Rayburn. It tempted me to make a harsh and perhaps foolish remark. But are you really engaged, Miss Ray- burn, to this—er—friend across the sea?" _

The question *as put so abruptly that for a moment Ella was nonplussed. Then reCovering her composure, she said: - "Why do you ask me that, Mr. Cartleigh ? " "Oh, I, don't know," he answered, lightly; "but I'm interested in you, you know. If I thought that you were-" . He stopped short. "Well ? she observed, half-fearful that he would complete the sentence as she had completed it in her own mind. t'What were you about to say?" "Well, if I thought that you were disengaged, hang me if I wouldn't sail in and win you." There was something about his cheeky frankness that attracted the girl. She half-admired, too, his dogged perseverance, his determination to over- come her oppcsition. "Well," she said at length, engaged, Mr. _ Cartleigh, but----'
nut "what ? " "I cannot be false to Steve."
"I'm not formally
"False! Fiddlesticks!" exclaimed Cartleigh, for- getting himself in his impetuosity. "Beg pardon. I didn't mean that. How can you be false to him if you haven't made him any promise of marriage ? "
She inade no reply to this query, for she knew full well she had promised to marry Steve. She realised that she had gone too far. She had told this man too much.

"Come now," said her companion, "I don't think you care a very great deal about this—ah— friend of yours, do you?" "Steve is more to me than anyone else in the world," she replied, stoutly. This was a rebuff that Cartleigh was scarcely prepared for. "The young minx doesn't really care anything about the fellow," he assured him- self, "but evidently she won't admit it yet, and she won't have the precious Outlander run down. Egad! She is a paralysing puzzle / But I'll master her yet,"
lie changed his tactics. "Do you think kindly of me, Miss Rayburn?" he asked.

. The question was embarrassing to the girl. ' "I? Oh, yes. I scarcely know what to say, Mr. Ralph. • Yes, of course I do," she blurted Out. "You have been kind to me. I owe my life to you. You saved me from drowning at Christmas. Yes, I do think kindly of you, very kindly—as a friend.",

"As it friend," he repeated. Then in coaxing tones: "Don't you think you can think more and more kiiidly of me, as something more than a friend, Ella—lliss Rayburn ? " Then in low impassioned voice he continued: "I love you, Ella, I love you, and I want you to love me. You do love me but you are afraid to own it.
You--" _ "Mr. Cartleigh !" the girl cried, and she drew . _
back as, in his-frenzy, he-seized her by the arm. "You mustn't speak so, you mustn't! I shall leave you." She started to run down the field path, but he hurried forward and detained her.

"Listen, Miss Rayburn 1 You must hear me. I must have an answer. You must strive to like me. I'll make you like me," he cried, in passionate tones. "There, I forgot myself! I didn't mean that. You'll try to think 'kindly of me, though. You'll try, won't you?" "Oh, I don't know. Don't press me to speak, Mr. Cartleigh." She was very excited and flurried. "Of course I like you. I have told you so," she said, after a pause. "But you must not ask me to like you better than Steve. I fear—l fear—" The ' sentence was not completed. A man came suddenly upon them, and, as Ella recognised Ben, the warehouseman, her white face flushed guiltily. ,"Good neet," cried Ben, cheerily, and passed quickly on. The couple walked along in silence. Cartleigh was desirous of following up the slight advantage he felt he had already gained, but he could scarce trust himself in his then uncommonly excited condition.

He was consumed with a desire to possess this weaver lass, to have her for his plaything, to have her amenable to his every whim and desire. She was weak and fickle. She did not know her own mind. She could not truly interpret her own feelings. That she had a liking for him she had now clearly stated. And this meant much, meant more than she herself would admit. And she "feared "—what? Feared that if she allowed her true feelings towards him to sway her she would give herself wholly to him and discard Stephen Hart. Such were Ralph Cartleigh's reflections, and he had accurately diagnosed Ella's feelings in regard to himself and her absent lover.

Month by month, by reason of Steve's dis- couraging letters, by her mother's constant reitera- tion of the necessity of making "a good match," by reason of Ralph's assiduous attentions, she found herself more surely becoming drawn towards the factory-master's son. "We'll be good friends, anyhow, Miss Rayburn," said Ralph, as they were about to part near Ella's home. "Whether you will or will not think kindly of me I shall ever think kindly of you, yea, more than kindly—lovingly. Good-night, dearest," And pressing her hand warmly he hurried away. "Who is yon 'at you've bin talkin' to ? " asked widow Rayburn, as her daughter entered the house. "I heard you talkin' to some'dy." "It was Mr. Cartleigh." "Mr. Cartleigh, say you! Haven't you got beyond th" mister' stage yet? I should have thought you'd have bin callin' him Ralph' by this time. Eh, lass, if I'd got no forrader with my courtin' nor you've done, I should have bin a single woman to this day." "Then I shouldn't have been here," said Ella; "and perhaps that would have been better for all concerned."

"Hey-day What's to do now 'at you're so down in th' dumps an' takin' such a gloomy view o' life? Is th' weavin' bad, or th' courtin' ? Th' courtin', I reckon. Well, for myself, I should think Mestur Ralph a nice sort of a chap to court .with. If I'd had such chances as you've had I'd have nipped him up long since." "Why do you talk like that, mother," said the girl, sharply. "There's no question of courting so far as Mr. Ralph and I are concerned. Because I happen to be in his company occasionally I don't see why you, at any rate, should jump to such conclusions. Mr. Cartleigh is no more to me than any other male friend in Dalesworth." "Th,en he ought to bee" said Mrs. Rayburn, spiritedly, "and would be if you didn't keep botherin your head about that chap abroad as will never be worth a sixpence if he lives- to be as owd as Methuselah, it's my opinion. Mestur ought to be more to you than any other friend, l'll tell you. Friend, indeed He ought to be your husbant by now, an' would have bin if you'd bin any other lass in Dalesworth but yoursel'. I can tell you, Ella, what you know yoursel', that there's not a lass in th' town but would jump at th' chance of weddin' Ralph Cartleigh, wastrpl,as he is an' all, as some folks reckon. A'ni gere you've got th' chance, first chance, afore. anybody else, an you make nowt of it seen-tin:ly.. a time will come when you'll wish you had done, take my word for it. A bird in hand is,worth two in th' bush. You make sure of tlx' cliap'itsis here an' ne'er bother about t'other as 'lEi gallivantin' about in a savage country." The voluble dame rattled on for a considerable time in the same strain, extolling, the virtues of the factory-master's son and depreciating the one-time " big-piecer. " She was determined that so far as she could influence matters her daughter should marry Ralph Cartleigh. With this end in view she would injure Stephen Hart's chances as far as possible. The letters sent from South Africa were the chief links bindine toeether the two lovers. This Widow

Annual Distribution of Prizes.

-- The annual distribution of prizes in connectief; with the Warrington Ragged School took place Sunday. It being the first anniversary of the op 0121: lag of the new premises, the committee dedidedtri, commemordte the same by presenting to Sex' scholar on the books a Bible, bearing a suitable scriptiort instead of, as customary, Selecting those who have made the requisite number of at- tendances. Tb 9 PRESIDENT of the institution (Mr. J. C. Parr). 5'4 he bad been asked to perform a very pleasing ducY.Sti s't be the medium for presenting to each child a preSi which had been provided by those who took so stal!l interest in the school and in the children who attend= and who devoted so •nuch time and trouble to the structien of the little flock. He would first of all addroP the children with words of welcome and encouragenroo It was pleasant to see Bopp an orderly. quiet, attentieb and intelligent assembly of little Amu gathered in fro,lig the most necessitous and least attractive part of tw town, children whose chief claim and recomelendatiall't If he might so express it, was teat they were very to° very needy, and lacking in the ao vantages and ordieari comforts—they mighty 'alhaost nay the necessities-1; decent healthy life. Be would tell them that thougb world might seem hard to them that they were much under the care of the Almighty 03c1 e. AnY ° their more fortunate neighbours, and that with the sistance of the kind friends who were looking after the, if they tried to be good and honest, and well conduote" they would become goon and useful members of ',Jell and able to earn their own living respectably a°,o honourably. In order to help them in the Pi they should tread the present they w3re receive to-day would be their guide and their suppor;ig To be able to read was already a great sVp on the roaa education, and if they read their Bible attentively tiler would find in it all the knowledge they would need teach them what they ought to do and what they ooP", not to do. He would like, before sitting down, to c0,1:1; gratulate these earnest and energetic workers on improved condition and prospects of their good From very modest and small beginnings they had sraie°„d up that ragged school to an important positon 'in t", town, and as its premises were larger and more CO modious, let them hope that its influence and good viar4o might increase in like proportion. Their aim was to Tea`:o those who were not brought within the sphere of otl3°A educational institutions,and rescue those little ones frol' ignorance, or what was worse than 15;noratIli vicious teaching, who could not be reaeli by other organisations and by inculcating habitS order and discipline, and cleanliness and atteatiell,n rules, set them on the right road to become happy,usetw respectable, self-supporting members of the comnalla% Mrs. Penn presented the Bibles (over 200). Thu I, were also present :—Mesdames R. Goreett and Gunnell, and Mr. and Mrs. Fanshaw. Letteis of ap0.,,,c'0, for non-attendance were received from Mr. and mak Robert Davies, Mr. R Garnett, and Mr. J. Lyon Villittt Two of the scholars were specially praised (Wite afit.6- Mary A. Titchard) for their singing of solos. At terP't., distribution short addresses were delivered by NT-s. g nett, Mr. Skelland, Mr. Osborne (joint ffnioders of first ragged scholn Dal:aril-lane 13 years ago), and Fanshaw. Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee. The Extension of the Volunteer Quarters At a meeting held on the 8111 March, the committee placei on !word an expression of deep regret on the loss of the valuable services of the Deputy-Chairman, and of sympathy with his relatives in their bereavement. It was resolved that Ald3rman Wright be appointed a member of this committee, and Councillor Smethurst deputy-chairman, that the alterations of the baths be proceeded with and tenders obtained for the work, and that the tender of the Warrington Slate Company,Ltd., to supply patent Victoria curbs for the walk round the fountain be accepted, and that the plans now submitted by Major Roomy, adjutant, for extension of the volun- teer quarters, be approved, subject to the plan of the elevation being submitted for approval. Alderman BOLTON, in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the committee, alluded to the iresolution on page 18 of the Council's minutes with reference to the extension of the Volunteer quarters. He said that Major Roome had submitted more plans, but they were prac• tically the same, except with reference to the alteration in front of the gable to face the Park. He expected all the arrangements would prove to be perfectly satisfac- tory. The estimates were practically the same as last year, except that they had had to put on £6OO for elec- tric lighting, decorating, and other purposes. Councillor SMETRITIOT seconded, and the motion was agreed to. Market Extensions and Improvements.

Alderman Eitereninsex,in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the Markets Committee,said there was an in- crease in'the income from the markets almost every week. They had for many years considered the practicability of carrying out the original scheme of covering in that por- tion of the market extending from Marnet-street to Walker's Brewery, and that work was included in their estimates for the coming year. It would, when com- pleted, protect the stallholders and those who paid toll. With regard to that portion of Queen-street which had been acquired of late, it was proposed to cover it over for the benefit of wholesale and retail produce dealers. The pavement which bad been put down was very, much appreciated, and they felt sure that an increased income to the Committee would be the result of the addditional covering in of the market. There was, the Alderman explained, an increased expenditure in consequenee of electric lighting. Couneillor ROGERS seconded. Alderman SUTTON thought it was a pity the work sq.= gested was not done some time ago when it could have been done at half the cost. It should have been done then or the committee should have waited until a better opportunitY presented itself. Councillor LEE rose to explaie that be did not think the committee ought to be blamed. The matter bad been under consiieratiln for two or three years. Alderman HI7TCIINSON : Six years. Councillor LEE : Alderman Sutton ought to under- stand a subject before Le speaks. (Laughter.) At the above committee's meeting, on March 22nd it was resolved that the design for lamp-posts now submit- ted by Mr. Preecebe approved, and that four additional street lamps be erected in the four main streets in the 1 positions pointed out by the committee. A letter having been received from the Acting Conservator of the River 1 Mersey with respect to the proposed' sewer outfall from the non works into the Mersey, it was resolved that the 1 proposed drain be connected with the geyser in Parr-street. A letter having been received from the 1 seeretary of the Lancashire Electri3 Power Company 1 with a copy of the Bill amended in accordance with the undertaking given by the Company to the President of the Board of Trade on second reading, and which now only contains power for the company ttrcarry their mains through one district in order to reach another district, and power being reserved to local authorities to determine the route and to carry out the work at the cost of the company, it was resolved that on the com- pany giving a clause not to oppose any future extension of the borough boundry, and to cease to supply within the extended area on terms to be mutually agreed upon or in default to be settled by arbitration, the Cofpora- don will net appear on the petition presented against the Bill. A SATISFACTORY BUDGET. Reduction of the Sewers Rate. The Couued tha proceeded to the consideration of tho estimates of exp nditure and incom for the year c unmencing, the Ist April, 1900, in other 'monis, " The Budget." The folio ging is a brief summary of the esti- mates for 1897, 1893, 1899, and 1900 :- 2 s. d. a. d. s. d. April, 1898. April, 1899. £370537 1-36224 5 4...40591 11 11 The imprevement rate was fixed at 2s 8 in tne £, and the general Rowers rate at 21, each to be collected by two half-yeatly instalments. Alderman FAIRCLOUGU said before presenting the estimates he would like to say that generally speaking •the committee hid kept witbin the estimates for the last year. In two cases, the health and the hospital, unfore- seen creumstatiCs hsd arisen which had necessitated extra exlee nditere. Notification of infectious diseases, disinfectants and extra wages of men disinfectinee, placarding the town, & , caused he overspending by the Health Department of £297. The Hospital overspent £506 ;r1 providing extra staff for the increased number of patients and provisions for same. The General Purposes Com inittee eversp Int their estimate by £328. Preliminary ch.rges re tramways, achertisine, tei me, inquiry re county boroneh, election of borough auditors, were accountable for this. In the Town Hall department £2BO were over-spent as fellow : Alterations at Town Hall not in estimate, £156; amount expended on tea room over estimate £5B; alteration to Water Works Office, £6O. It would, perhaps, appeir somewhat strange that although th s estimates in the total had been increased by £4,367 the rates should net have gone up accordingly. There were two or three reasons to account for this. The overseers were prepared to meet the extra call upon the borough rate without increasing the rate. In the improvement rate they had a balance of £2,000 in hand, principally saved by the alteration in the mode of repayment of loans, which together with the increasing produc- tiveness of the rate was estimated to pro -luce the re- quired amount. A, balance on hand in the sewers rate had enabled them to reduce this rate to 21., and in all probability they would be able to keep this rate at 2d for the next year. Full provision had been mae!re tor al' requirements of the several committees, and in no in- stance had anythine been struck out which was consi- dered absolutely necessary. He now proposed the follow- ing nobtioes .--(1) That the Council hereby estimate the amount of £16,382 1.2 s '2d, will, in aldition to the Boroogh Fund, be revired and sufineient for the per. poses to bleb the Borough Fund is applicable, under the Municipal Corporations Act, 1882, or otherwise by law, for the year to end 314 March, 1901; (2) that the Council do hereby order a borough rate to be made in pursuance of the Municipal Cerporatiens Alt, 1882, in order to raise the said amount ; (3) that the overseers of the township of Warrington be and they are hereby or- dered to pay to the treasurer of the borough, by instal- ments, and on or before such dates as may be fix id b; the Finance and E .tate Committee, th coot • ibution of the sum of £16,382 12s 21 out of the poor rate made or to be made for the said township of Warrineton, as pro- vided by the Municipal Corporations Act, 1882. Councillor Monsa seconded, and the resolutions were carried. Alderman FAIRCLOUGR then moved that the estimate for an improvement reef, as recommended by the Finance and Eitate Committee be confumed and that the Finance and Estate committee do make an improvement rate accordingly at two shillings and eightpence in tee polled, to be collected by two half-yearly instalments, and be authorized to affix the Common Seal of the Cor- poration thereto. Councillor las second d. Alderman FAIRCLOUOR also moved "That the estimate of the general sewers rate as recommended by the Fin- ance and Estate Committee be confirmed, and that the Finance and Estate Committee do make a general Sewer's rate accordingly at twopence in the pound,t) be collected by two half-yearly instalments, and be authorized to affix the Common Seal of the Corporation thereto." Councillor Lae seconded. The MAYOR said before the resolution was put he should like to say that the Council !lad every occasion to congratulate itself upon the present financial position of the Borough. In !laying this he knew that they were with him absolutely in the feeling of regret that the par- ticular member of the Council who had for so many years introduced the Budget (Councillor Shaw Green) was not present on that pleasant occasion to take part in the deliberations of that meeting. (Hear, hear.) Looking at the fact that their expenditure had neces- sarily increased very oonsiderebly, and that they had in front of them a !mentor of nkessary and desirable tin- prov6tnentg, ha did think it spoke Voluinteg for tho efficient management of the affairs of the town that in the face of this extraordinary expenditure they were able to reduce the general rates of the boroueh by 21. in the £. He thought it also established credit for the careful statement of fact which had characterized the members of that Council with regard to the improve- ments which were projected last year,and which entitled them to the claim of being able to put facts before their commt§ hich mieht be 'relied Upon as being thorOilehly accurate. He thougno he might fairly say they had every reason to congratulate themselves. Alderman &Inng said he agreed with the remarks which the , Mayor had just made. He wag also very agreeably disappointed with the Budget, Fie came there prepared to accept a large increase in the estimated ex- penditure during the present year. He thought at least they would have had soiree little addition to the rates but he was very pleateed indeed to find instead of that the figures were slightly in the other direction. He quite agreed that all who had had to do With the control of the finance arrangements were deserving of their best thanks. (Hear, hear.) C3UOCillor LEE said he quite agreed with everything that had been said. It was a matter' of cougratulation to nit concerned. The resolutions were then put and carried unani- mously. The Salary of the Medical Officer of Health'. Alderman SUTTON moved the following resolution : To determine the appointment of, and make a fresh appointment of, Mr. John Hankinsen Gorman, the medical officer of health for the borough, at a salary of £2OO per annum, under the provisions of the General 'Oilier of the Local Government Board, dated ths 23rd of March, 1891. He said it was not necessary to say mach about the question, as it was a formal one to enable them to appoint Dr. Gornall in such a manner that they could get back half his salary from the county instead of the corporation having to pay the whole of eit themselves. He would not submit the resolution as printed, but move first that Dr. Gornall be appointed medical Officer. :The MAYOR seconded and the motion was carried. Alderman SUTTON then moved that Dr.Gornall's salary be 200 per annum,

An Improvement to be made in Horsemarket Street. In accordance with notiee of motion Alderman FRAN- COMB in•evel that in the opiaion of thie C•iueeil the time ' h Is arrived for the reinov it of the premises at the corner of Lenne-strisee and Horseinarke-street, and that the Fivance Committee be requested to give notice to quit to the tenants thereof. He thought is, was pretty well known to everyone where these premises were situ ate. They knew that at the corner of L rrue-street, and Liorsemarket-street the theroughtare was very narrow , and the footpath was little more than a yard wide. His opinion in the first instance was that they ought to cut a ehce clean off, And thus make the street in future in , line with eleesrs. Skeltorees shop,but he had heard a good many opieione expreesed during the pure year, an geuerally these appeered to be tnat they ought to take down the property in Lynae- street. That s'reet was very narrow and there wa a tremendous amount of traffic upon it. As far es Horse- marke -streetwas cencerned it was positively dangerous. He had seen many narrow escapes and accidents, and also every day he had to step out into the road to allow' someone to pass him, or someone had to step into the road to let him pass It was almost impossible for any one to 8t5111(1 and look at the window ot the hoot shop. His idea of only cutting a piece off and building up the front was the outcome of a desire not to put the town to a lot of expense. But he found the Local Government Board bad already senctioned the borrowing of the money for taking this property down, and if there was one spot in the town that wanted widening more than another he thougnt it was this paetioular corner. He found this property was purchased in 1895, so they had had a censielerahle amount of time to think about the improvement. He thought they ought really to make up th, it minds to do it as quickly as possible. He was eery pleaeed to see the improvements going on along Wilderepool-road and Bridge-street, and he thought it would be the wisest policy the Corporation could adopt to make up their minds at once and face this difficulty in Horsemarket-street. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Heatrote seconded the resolution. This par- ticular spec, he said, was a very narrow place,especielly on Wedriesdays. (LAuetater ) It was the only piece of property that it was necessary for them to pull down in treat part, and he thought it ought to be removed en- tirely and a oroper street made. It was a very sharp corner, and conveyances coming in opposite directions were in danger of colliding with each other. He had had the place under close observation for some time. Alderman BOLTON said he would like to know why the Finance Committee were keeping the property up. Was it because it paid five per cent. on the money paid for it ? He thought it would be to the interest of the town to pull the property down. The property was bouelit with tint object in view. Alderman Fairtpeouon observed that the property was bringing in 5 pr cent., and the Corporation now inten- ded to take it away from them. Alderman BOexciez said it showed that the Finance Committee were simply a committee for signing cheques, and tley did not is now their awn business. They bought the property for the purpose of widening the street, and they forgot what they purchased it for, and tried to get all the moley out of it they could. Alderman SUTTON said he had always been of opinion • this property should come down for street improvement, but at the same time he thought as there had been such delAy in the in etter it might just as well remain in abeyance a little longer. There could be no harm dine by it. There were so many improvements in hand that they scarcely knew what they were about. He thought a very oppertone time to have approached this question would have been when they had Bridge-street finished, and the corner of Mr. Johnsoa's shop completed. At the same time, he was not going to oppose the resolution, because he was only too pleased when improvements _ _

could be made satisfactorily, Councillor F R ROBERTS inquired as to how much of this street was involved. He thought they ought to know what was included in the improvement. If it were onle intended to remove one shop be did not see the use of passing the resolution. Councillor Hes:rm./ observed that the next shop to the corner was included. Cowelllor LEE slid he could not understand Alderman Fr ,ncemb. At first he wanted to take the corner off,and thoe he wanted to take it right out so far as their pro- perty was concerned. If he did that he would have to buy the beerhouse besides. He doubted that they were going to make any ireprovecnent at all, considering they got £l5O a year for this property. There appeared to he a hunered and one things very much more important than this. If Alierman Frei:month wanted th- corner taken riff he die not, mind supporting him, but if he wanted to go right uo the street and destroy this £l5O he could not support him. Councillor BENNETT s sid h. di =s •ciated himself entirely from the parsimonious poicy whin hal been advocated by Alderman Fairclough, and to some extent by Coun- cillor Lee. AllerM4l3 FAIRCLOUGH : I have not said anything at all. (Laughter.) The MAYOR: I don't think Councillor Bennett is entitled to ref ir to his speech as yet. (Renewed laugh- ter ) Councillor BENNETT : If lem too hosty I will with- draw. The MAYOR It is a mere statement of fact. Councillor BENNETT • I don't think it was. The MAYOR : Tree Aldermsa has not a iiressed the Council. It was a sotto voce observation. CollitalOr BENNETT: It Was a very disorderly pro. ceeeing. lam surprised that the Alderman was guilty of such behaviour. (Laughter.) Continuing, Councillor Bennett said he did not think there was one improve- ment in the town more necessary tears the one proposed. He hardly th iught that the imerovernent in Bridge-st. was more important, because the danger of the projec- tion in Horsernerk,et-street could not be exaggerated. The ides of simply taking off the end was a question of being penny wise and pound foolies which those who were able to look ahead invariable deprecated. While they were dein; a job he was of opinioa that it should be done thoroughly. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR did not think there was any difference of opinion about the necessity for an alteration ; it was simply a matter of time. It would boa mistake to allow the property to remain up a day longer than they could possible help. (Rear, hear.) He should, therefore, support the motion. Alderman FAIRCLOUGEE said he had no objection to the property co Elea, down provided the interests of the Corporation were looked after. Councillor MONKS said the property was purchased in a sense illegally,and i was only recently that they ,ob- tained the sinction of the Loco' Government B Aril to borrow the money. That was the main reasen the matter had not been dealt with at an earlier date. The pullieg down of the property would improve the busi- ness premises in close contiguity, and these people who would benefit should help to face the cost an i not let it fall on the general holy of ratepoyers. (Hear, bear.) The MAYOR : That question will not he lost sight of. The prieciple of betterment was granted in our Bill last year; and in connection witn thus removal it will be taken into consideration. (Cries of " Vote.") Councillor SMETHURST ; One word in reply to Alder- man Sutton. Alderman FAIRCLOUGLI : I think you hal better be quiet. (Laughter.) Couloillor Selenetillee : I arc quite able to stand my cicrll Cotter. A. fortnight ago only, four persons were in 1 conveyance and they were rein into aid thrown out all ' of a heap. The lilies of people shere'd he tak-n into con- sideration. Alderman HITTCHINiON : Would it not be well to Cut off the corner an I keep the other premises which might bring in £7O or £BO a year to the Corporation ? Alderman Sterroo : What is being pulled down ? The MAYOR The whole of the property beloneiog to the Coreeration. Councillor MONKS Will there be More than one abogi taktn down ? , Councillor ALFRED JOLLEY : Two shops. The MAYOR: I think I have already explained that we own certa:n property at the corner of Lyme-street and Hars,qm‘rket-3treet—two shops and offices above. The motion 15 te remove the whole of that property. Al ierman FeeNCOMB in repie said he wished is to be understood that his resolution included the removal of the whole of the Corporation property. It was impoe- Bible to remove a portion only. The resolution was put t 3 the meeting and carried. Councillor Lee (who wished to propose an amendment but was ruled out of order) was the only dissentient. The Council tlesia rose.

MR. GUY REYNOLDS IN LADYSMITH. Story of the Siege. Great Hardships. Mrs. Sylvaraue Reynolds, Whetcrett Hall, near North- with, has received the following interesting letters from her Hen. Guy who was ha Ladysmith throughout the siege, and is a Lieutenant in the stti Dragoons. His brother is in the Imparial Yeomanry. Ladysmith N ov. 7, 1899. My dearest Mother.—l will write •a few lines to-day tho' when you will get them (if ever) Heaven knows. The railway is in possession of the Boers and we are in a state of siege, ani shall be so until we are renaved by the Army Corps, which cannot be for some time yet. We are not having a good time by any means. Shells are pouring into the town all day, and every day, and though they do not do mach damage their moral effect is pretty strong. It is not at all a pleasant sensation to hear a shell whistling towards you—not knowing where it will land or whether it will burst or not. Toe Cavalry Brigade had rather a nice little fight a few days ago. I fancy we must have killed a good many Boers witia our Shrapnel shells. We lost a few men. My sevradron was escort to tee gone and as we galloped up to take a position, their artillery opened fire a shell and missed my head by about a yard, and buried itself in the ground about 7 yards behind my horse, vinirre it burst and a plecco hit Captain Hoare, of my regiment, on the head knocking him off his horse. I rode back and carried him off into a watercourse. He had a nasey scalp wound , which I bound up till the doctor arrived. I think he will soon be all right again. As I write this a shell has just dropped about 30 yards from my tent, making a huge hole in the ground I saw Mary and lone two or throe times, but they have been ordered out of the town, and have, I suppose, gone to Durban. Only a very few inhabitants, are left here. At one time there were reported to be 25.000 Boers round the town, out I fancy lots of them have gone now, but their big guns are all retrial the town, and they keep us lively. lAM very fit and well in spite of very hard work an] very little sleep. WP are often out for 24 hours together, and sleep almost always in our clothes. I feel very dirty, a bath being an unknown luxury. The drinking water is about the colour of Mheley water. It is a very healthy place, and there is ,1 little or no siekness. I'm afraid you must be anxious I at present, getting no news of us, hut I hope we shall best them back soon and retake the railway and tele- grape. I will post this as soon as possible wad you may get it about Christmas. lam afraid we shan't be in Pretoria for Christmas, as we hoped, and we have lots of hard work before us yet. All the bulk of the fighting must be in Natal, as the Transvaal and Free State are entirely unsuited to Boer medes of fighting. Their artillery are really epleadid,but the rifle shooting is bad, I'm glad to say, or I'm afraid I shouldn't be writing this. Several times I must have been hit if they could shoot straight; I don't mind the bullets, but I don't care about the shells. All my love my dearest mother,—Ever your most loving sent—Gun. 21st November. All right up to now, but the heat is terrible, and they shell us all day and night now. All love, GUY. In continuation, sth December,—We are still here be- ing besieged, but hope we shell soon be relieved now. We hear that the Boers have been beaten at Mooi River about 40 or 50 miles from here. ,They will have, of couree, to mond the railway which the enemy has blown up, but it can only be a matter of a week or ten days now before they come close enough for us to make a combined attack, in which case we hope to capture a lot of the Boer guns. They have altogether 30 guns in position, all shelling the town and camps. Only two days ago a shell burst in the hospital, killing one and wennling nine men. A man had his leg carried away below the knee. He was standing only five yards from me. One sees some dreadful sights. We have been here five weeks to-day, fool is gettiue scarce and any sort of luxuries are quits ruinous. Eggs (not fresh) 61 to is each, I hear of one man paying £5 for 100 cigarettes We have no drink of any sort left except tea and a lot of rum once a week. We hear of great victories on the Cape Colony side, and hope they were really decisive. I think we have had all the herd work here in Ladysmith and thi t we have really broken the back of the war, be keeping a large force of the Boers round the town and also by draw- ing away all their artillery. I could fill a book in relating narrow escapes and little events of the war, but we don't get much time to write. To-day lam orderly officer and remain in caino, so I have a bit of time. I have been mentioned in despatches by Me Claim and- ing Officer for good service done out patrolling, but whore every one has done so well, it is but a small dis- tinction,andl have done no more than anyone else or more than my duty. I rather wish I had made arraneements to send a weekly letter to some Warrington paper. My name would have made it interesting to Warrington people. Please let everyone know lam very well nue I cannot fled time to write to all,though I have done so to one or two. I had fever for a few days when the heat first earns on, but I haee eshatten it off and am fit for anything now. We shall have, I expect, one really big battle before we leave here and I've no doubt we shall give them a good licking and after that the war will soon be ovsr, though they win make a stand here and there, perhaps at Heidelberg and Pretoria. I hope you are all getting through the winter well and that it is a mild one. I suppose Syl will soon be setting off. I hope hell have a good time. I hope you get good news from Beaty and Inns, Give them my love when yoe write. I m ost stop now, dearest mother. Withal( my love and wishes for Christmas and the New Year (though this will arrive a bit late for ben.) I think of you all At home constently and hope it won't be long bsfore we are together again.—Ever your lovine son, GUY. 7,h January, 1900, Ledeemith.

Mc dearest Mother,—Jut a few lines to tell you I am very well. I wire you the day before Christmas I hope you got it all right. We had a tremendous battle yesterday. The Boers attacked Ladysmith in a very braye.manner and actually at one time drove our men back,from a ridge whieh is the strongest position we have. The Cavalry were ord,red out dismounted to to inforce the Infantry and then we were able to drive them back. lam now in command of a Maxim gun and was able to get it into action and I am very glad to say it did splendid work and drove the Beers back from that part of the hill and killed a good number. The bullets whistled pretty thick round us. One hit a bit of mud in front of my face (as I lay down) covering me with mud and water. Our losses killed must be nearly 150 and probably 300 woended. Tne Boers are estimated at 500 or 600, but I think not so many. The General and the Colonel were good enough to report favourably on me, and I feel very proud. We expect another attack to- night and hops it will come off as we are much stronger and better defended, but we could hardly stand general attacks as our men are weak and most of them ill. TVey have been on half-a-pound of meat and half-a- pound of bread a day, and no drink (but water) for some time. About 30 per cent are in hospital. I keep very well and my heart seems stronger than it has been for some time. We ought to be relieved now within 10 days as the Boers are retiring from in front of Buller and two columns are reported to be threatening their flanks, and also to cut off their lines of retreat. It pours with rain almost every afternoon and gets us thoroughly wet so that 'ie.! may enjoy a really cold night, and it is cold waiting and watching for Mr. Bier to creep up. I hear a lot of ?dilitia, arm corning out, I wonder if the 4th and 23rd are coming ? Poor Plate,e,nephew of the Colonel's in my regiment.died yesterday of enteric. He was a vary nice boy, and we all liked him very much. I can't tell you how glad we shall all 1:3,1 to be relieved,to be able to go for a walk or a ride without being shelled from all sides, and to get some food—not trek-ox and biscuit and dirty water,also some letters and papers, to hear what you have been dQing and thinking all this time practically 10 we.lre to day. I expect people have often been ineoug as to the fate of Ladysmith. We knew they could never take it, but their shells have been annoying, and men have been sick with no exercise and bad water. No more news °OW. I Must go end strengthen the place where my Maxim gun Innae they attack. Will write again soon,:when the line is open,—.A!!m love to my dearest mother. Ever your loving son, GO% January 30, 1900.—My DArest IVlother.—l sea 9, letter to you by a Kaffir runner some days ago but as iita had to go through the Boer lines you may not have received it. I hope you did, as it will make you feel

easy about me. I Will continua this more as a diary than a letter. When I wrote you we were hoping that all had gone well with the relieving column and if it had we should in all trohability be relieved by now, But hough they took the position all right they allowed a few Bo `l6 to calve them back from it. Of coarse we haven't heard details but it seems unpardonable that a force allowed itself to be driven out of a position after once taking it. Either they took no precautions, ani were surprised or else they wouldn't face the Blers. In either case they are terribly to blame. It seems that the only good fighting troops are the Indian Contingent who have almost all been on service before and who are all locked up here and are in such a weak spate that it will take a long time before they recover, if they ever do. All the regiments here (with very few exceptions) have shown conspicuous gallantry whenever they have met the enemy and it is a great pity that Such a splendid division should have had to be sacrificed, though it has undoubtedly saved Natal. We have had bad weather lately and get wet through pretty well every night, and it is very miserable and cold, and bad news on the top of it all makes one rather low spirited. Buller seems to be so dreadfully slow, and our men are dying in num- bers every day, also the horses, which get only about 41b. of grain a day and are fading away. I hear they are going to destroy 500 of the worst so as to give more food to the others. This war will cost the country a nice little sum before it is all'Otrer and afterwards they'll have to re-organise the army, especially the Artillery, in some way or other.—either compulsory volunteering or compulsory Militia,! expect. Our Artillery, except the siege train, has been absolutely Unable to cope with the enemies' guns. It seems very hniiiiliating to us, during any of these battles, that the SOers, who are not mach better than savages, should be
