div.p: able to hold us easily at arm's length. They have also a 'better rifle than ours. The old men, I fancy, shoot as well as ever they did, but the youne?.r men are not very good, theager they are not by any mans to be despised. It seems a marvel to me no v I look back at Eland's Laegte battle. At 200 yards tee B iers fired hundreds of rounds at myself and four men and only grazed a bergs, B,nte then there have been men bowled over with great regularity at 2,000 yards. 6'h February.—A,iother week gone and no nearer relief. For the last three nights we have all been waiting for an attack from the Beere The Intelligence Department have—or think they have—good iriformation that the enemy will make one more desperate attempt to take Ladysmith, and if they attack in great numbers we shall have all our werk cut out to beat them off, but I think we shall do it all right. At all events we are ready to them and they'll hare a warm le eeption if they do came. If they are decisively beaten in their attack I fancy they'll raise the seige and retire north to some strong position, probably Laing s N de or Majube Hill in which case we shall be relieved without Bulltr's help. He was fighting the day before yesterday but we have not heard the result yet. I trust he was not beaten again. We have to live almost entirely on horse fl7.eh and 2ilbs a day. I don't care for horse much ;it is rather sweet and generally very tough, though the ox is not much bettsr in that respect. There is no more news this week, but if we are attacked again I hope to be able to send you an account of it. 10th February.—We have heard Buller's guns going hard for the last 4 dies, but he is apparently no nearer day by day. I expect the Boers have taken no some very strong positions. He is only about 10 or 12 miles from hero so we can hear him plainly, and shall be able to see the Boers retreat if he can only manage to teat them. We complete our 100:n day of siege to-day, though we have been shelled for over that period : it is 100 days since the railway was cut. Our Generals expect to be relieved in a very few days now, but it all depends on wh ther Buller can drive the enemy back or not. It has been terribly hot the last few days, and enteric is very bad. We lost 3 men in the regiment yesterday. No more news to-day I believe we have got rations—of sorts—for over 3 weeks more, but if Buller can't relieve us this time we may as well make up our minds to cepitulate. I suppose we should hang on till we were sterved out, or the Boers might wtack in large numbers and after a while we should be obliged to give in, as we have hardly any ammunition tor our Artillery left. We should ot course, lose a tremendous lot of men, and the Reeitnent would be made prisoners and I suepese be sent to Pretoria, though I donut if the Boers could feed us there. However, I expect Buller will manage to relieve us before very long, and then I expect all the Ladysmitn garrison will be sent to some healthy place for a month to recover their sttength and health. After that I hope they'll let u 3 have another go at the Beers' as we have had all the diagreeable part of the war, without any of the fun, exsespt Eland's Laagte, which seems years ago. I'm afraid the Innes will have had all their horses Set ,cornmaiideered by the Boers, and I fancy he will be lucky if they haven't spoilt his bodge for him. They have played the dickens in mot houses:in Nttal. 18th February.—Still no signs of relief. We are all beginning to feel weak and slack. We only get ilb of bread now. To stop the gaps I bought a bottle of cod liver oil the other thy for £l. I can't say am fond of it, but it is something to swallow. We eat mules now, and I think these rather better than horsfebut there ain't much in it. I managed to get foot eegs the other day at 4s 6i each ; they were splendid. Beller had another try to relieve Us the other day but cede i atrain for the third time. Now I suppose we most wait till Roberts marches through the Free State and qtrettens to cut off these Boers. This will take a Itne time bet they say now that we have rations for 60 days—thoueh I doubt if many would live for that long on ilb of bread and some horse or mule Beth—we should be able to hold ont. The danger is that ecurve noisy break out. At present there are qtet• 2,000 :ay of 10,000 in hospital and we cannot afford to lose any more men, if we are to hold the place. I think the Beers could take Lady- smite if they could induce their men to attack in great numbers. We hole eleven mnetcit outpatte, and have very few Intel in reserve. I see in an old paper that Potter has got a commission in the 10th Hussars, so I suppose Bii's trio is off. I shou'd like to do a bit of a sea trip when this is ever to pink up. I expect the Reriment will he sent straight hack re India when we have had a bit of a rest. filet- have oaten all except about 130 of our hori,e3 and teey will sten be finished. No more now. 20:h February—Bullet has, after four days' fighting. taken Bingen Mountain, which I can s, e as I write about 12 miles off. We :leant see greet numbers of our men on the hill this morning, and thee have now got some guns up there. We can hear the firing quite distinctly, but cannot see muen. Buller signals to say all is going well. Se nosy we hope we are really going to see the end, but one doesn't know. He ha e been almost as near before, and was driven back. Tins time, however, he has got a hdl whch commands their positions, and has got his big guns on it. Besides,s,ooo Free Staters left here when they heard of the relief of Benberley. Alto- gether the news to-night is good, and I hope we shall get something to eat I:Pfore long. I am raveoous. I wired to Frank today. I hope he sent you a cable. Too dark to write any mlre, hope to hear good news again to-morrow. Good-night. 23rd February.—At last we are gettieg good newreand plenty of it. To begin with, we are on almost full rations of biscuits and horse or trek-ox, so now we live again. This would not have been done unless relief were absolutely certain and very close. The general opinion thinks 3 or 4 days, and I hope a wsek at the out- side will see us relieved, though we shall not get stores for some days after that. A ereetet number of the Beers have left, and Buller thinks there are only 5,000 or so against him. His guns s iund very cies-. and their music is very pleasant to us after more than 16 weeks of siege. I still keep pretty wel but I are about as weak as a cat and find it a great effort te walk about much. I haven't had a night in bed for seven weeks now and it is too hot to get much sleep during the day. I ex- pect a great many will break down directly we are re- lieved, the reaction will tell on them The news of relief will come as very welcome to a great many people at home, and to the nation in general. What a terrible thing it woind have b0,.41 for the tirmv if she Beers haul captured the 10,000 odd men there are here. I think we are spared even the anxiety of that now, as Buller is keeping them rather too busy for there to think of attacking Us. It is exactly 5 months to-day since I sailed from Southampton. I little thought what we were in for then. I don't r xptet we shall get any stores Ste, for some few days after Buller arrives, as the line is sure to ba destroyed in several places and waggons cannot come very fast. I wired to Frank a day or two back to send us provisions by some reliable agent. He was very good to me wletn I arrived and I hope he'll do his best. I suppose winter will be over when you get this. From the few papers I have seen there seems to have been plenty of frost. I can't tell you how I look forward to getting letters from you all. I hope in a week from now we shell have received them, 3 months' news takes a bit of making up. 27th February.—Majube Day! We can hear Buller fighting and can see his shells bursting. 28th February.—The Beers are in full retreat. A. wire has just come from Buller retying he beat the Boers yesterday. So Majuba tray is avenged, think God! Cronje is captured and I believe the war is practically over: I can't deserlles the feeling of relief when we see these thousands of waggons and Boers retreating, and if we were only fit and well, couldn't the cavalry pursue. them! We should finish them off I firmly believe; I can hardly write. I feel quite bewildered, only yester- day we were put back to a ilia. of biscuit and 3oz. of mealie flour per day, and every one thought the worst had happened, and instead of that to day we get thia glorious TIMM We are to all intents Ind purposes. relieved and shall, I hope, soon see the last of this dreadful place—how we loath and detest it. I'm afraid, however, we shall see no more fighting. I shall try to get attached to some corps or other, as I want to go to Pretoria. "However, I want t) rest a night in bed and good food for a few days at all events. I shan't write any more now. I will write after a few days, but will send this for first post. I have just volunteered to go out and follow up the Boers. I'm afraid they'll be too fast for us, and perhaps we shan't go, but I want to 14ve a shot at them. Au Revolt my dearest panther, all nay love to you and all at home. lam very well aril. Tery happy to-day,—Eeer your loving sma: Gny.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football
[By "Ovp.list."]

Whatever chances Warrington had of winning the Northern Union Cup this smson were extinguished on Saturday at Rochdale. Only the worst of pessimists could have expected the cHeAt which was sustained at the hands of the Ilornets. Personally I had not the least doubt of Warrington's ability to conquer, and I think the eight or nine hundred anti:mil .tists wt o followed the team were of a similar opinion. Much WM held to depend on the weatner,for if there is any rain no ground can become unfit for play so rapidly as that. at Dane., street, Rochdale. But there was no rain on Saturday, and there had been none for some time previously, so that there was every reason for anticipating " a fair field and no favour."

Alas for the " fair field "! A more miserable mud swamp than that Warrington had to play upon could not have been found in tho length and breadth of England, and it is a burning shame that so iznp.,mat an event as a cup tie should have to be decided undEr such vile conditions. Thu ground is, I believe, on a lower level than the river, .which lies some 50 yards away, and no system of drainage can keep it dry. Probably there is no drainage at all. It any rate if there is it does not drain one iota. Notwithstanding the dry weather, the playing field was two or three inches deep in the stick- iest, slimiest black ooze imaginable. To make nv.tters look better the Hornets Committee had scattered a huge quantity of sawdust on top—as a sort of upper crust to the pie. Ten minutes play sufficed to churn the lot up into one disgusting, disheartening, disgracltul 1112$1. And thirty men haul to try to play scientific football in this. No wonder they faded, and no wonder the better side lost.

It would take a large-sized extra-strong phonograph to record all that Warringteniane thought when they saw the ground, and all they said when the match was finished. I heard some of the most sulphuric adjectives that our accommodating language provides a man with any imagination and a big grievance. There was some really fantastic swearing, and it is a great pity that the committte of the, Rochdale Hermits could not have had a special hearing of it all. It made an ordinary man's hair curl anti his blood run cold, but if it had driven some sense into the committeemen it would have cisme good service and perhaps been excused by the R,c ,rding Angel. The certainty that Warring- ton would have won under fair conditions was the bitterest, reflection, and the fact that the winners " get home " by a fluke did not soften the prevailing " leaki- ness." We have got to grin and bear it, however, I:sup- pose, though it tax.ei one's patience to think that for the second time Warrington' cup career has been cut short by the state of the ground they have had to play

To say that it is the same for both sides is no argu- ment for if the graund only had enough—as on Saturday—footbali is an ucter impossibility. A result may be arrived at, but not by football, and cups are meant to Ise won by football and nothing else. Such conditions bring the best teams down to a level with the worst, which is distinctly unfair. Uuder proper condi- tions there is a fair and suare struggle for supremacy and the best aide wins by the bast football. Some more stringent rules should be in force for serious matches with regard to the state at tie ground, and a protest by one of the clubs ought to have due weight with that arbiter of fate—the referee.

As the watch counts,l had better say something about the way it went. Th6re is not very much to be said,for any five minutes of the game would be a criterion of the whole. Rugby football, as we know it, was an im- possibility, and the game developed into kick and rush, mark and punt, etc. .oace or twice Warrington tried passing, and got the ball across all right, but the backs were so hampered by the mud they had to carry about with them that cumbined runs were out of the question. The homesters did not trouble much about science, but I plugged along in the style they have got used to in the Dane-street swamps. In this style the match dragged its weary length along to the disgust of the large crowd assembled. Neither side appeared to have any advantage and a draw appeared certain when an unfortunate incident occurred. Hallam, who bad got through an immense amount of work in splendid style failed to gather the ball near his line, and Wight- man scored smartly. I say the incident was unfor- tunate because it lost Warrington the match, and it was rough on Hallais after the excellent display he had gives. The Hernets got a biz slice of luck for they would never have scored otherwise and a bie drubbing was in store for them at Wilderspool, the following Wednesday. Fish made one brilliant run towards the close and would certainly have scored had the footing been good. As it was be was captured, and with heavy hearts the Warringtonians returned home.

Hallam was the best man on the field, apart from that one costly mistake. His fielding and kinking were superb, though he punted to the wrong wing rather fre- quently. Tne other Warringtottians were clearly net theinselve and not much can be said for them. They defended well and that was all. The teams were equally matched f lrward, and among the borne banjo, Rigg and Wightroan were the shiniuglfghts. Neither was brilliant but both were wood,eifinly safe, the former taking an the heart out 9 bill opPonents oy persistent marking. Platt vf?,i eVelltr4 undmtudy gt Imk,

word /or the ref r. Mr. Robinson (of Manning- ham) had charg- of the whistie and he let people know It. The Hornets bad about twenty free kicks and War- lingtoa had two. The Debi:Li 4 v•'Ara 2irea for off side, p«lncipally in connection with tlit, ..!VA yards rule. Either Mit. Robinson knew nothing ablut the rule or he had a very exaggerated idea of what five yards was. Many a time ho Inc/tight back the War:ingtn forwards after Aolancija gas; when they were t,D yards from the catcher. The Hornets ner:.r seemed tl be in trouble at all. but War- rington had a very hard time at Mr. Robinson's hands. Manningbara is the place for him; there is no opening fOr sect- nriginei rofereeing down here. But the Hornets , must like him—love him dearly perhaps—for he takee charge of their fortunes at a!ford to-day I 54149.

. RECEIVED intense en- The Queen and Ireland. thusiasin evel•yAliKe, and

giving the loyal a new chance of expressii:g their emotion, the QUEEN has reached and entered Dublin like a eceique:or. She has won the hearts of the Irish people. Tney are susceptible hearts, we all know, aLL,,ohed o their own country, their own songs, their own national customs and ideas. The QUEEN hRs recognised these things, and if the occasion comes late, it serves to show that what has.heen svd before vvas true, and that the blame rest's upon Ministers, and not on the QUEEN herself. If the QUEEN had taken as much notice of the Irish people as she has dons of the Scotch people, the Irish would have bees more loyal. A Royal residence ie Ireland has been advocated for years. The obsts.cles have never been on the part of the QUEEN and Royal Family. They have always come from the -Midst& and the play of parties for the time being. The point impresses itself upon us now that the QuEBN ' on her own initiative, has paid another visit to , Ireland and been so magnificently received. The people of Dublin and the people of Ireland have seized the right point of view. They are loyal to the Crown, they are loyal to the Sovereign, and beyond that we need not go at pn,sent. We do not ask them to forego any of their national feel- ings, for the simple reason that the present is not a political occasion. The QUEEN herself wished to pay a visit to Dublin, to show her admiration g the valour of her Irish soldiers, and she took the step without being advised by her Minif,ters. The Irish people quite understand this part of the case, and the attempt to make a special protest was quite unnecessary. The QUEEN would still be QUEEN of Ireland if Ireland were woiling under a Home Rule Constiiution, and so the idea of making a Nationalist protest may be regarded as an attempt to manufacture plitical capital out of what is not a political visit. Irish soldiers w-iuld be in the service of the Empire even if a National Parliament sat in Dublin and Mr. RIM" MOND were Prime Minister. The Irish people, however, were not much disturbed by these nice considerations on Wednesday. They were demon" strative, hearty, generous, passionately loyal. They showed an unstinted reverence for the venerable lady who, in her advancing years, had come over to see them, and to find that change which vraB denied to her by circumstances elsewhere. From Kingstown to Dublin Castle, what a proces' sion it was! The waving, wonderful crowd was all smiles, all cheers, all love and loyalty. Picturesque incidents attended the whole of the march. It was a triumphal pro- cession. The sentimental had their full swing 0 enjoyment. The calculators were entirely out ef it. The Irish people have one undoubted char' acteristic on these occasions—they are tremend" ously sincere. They surrender themselves to the feeling of the moment, and they leave us in no doubt of what they mean. Wednesday was Dublin's great day, and it was a great day for Ireland too. The people were not to be bustled by the politicians, and they took possession of , everything and everybody. To see the QUEEN, to cheer her, to let her see the proud hearts of her Irish subjects were in subjection and delighted ; homage to her public and private life, were the . great objects they had in view. And they were ' successful. It was indeed a wonderful day!

div.p: -that something like a general mobilisation of the I I.ussian army is in progress. In the southern Provinces these arrangements have been already made. They are of evil omen for the peace of the world. Russia has so many lines upon Which she can act that we cannot b e quite sure 'Where the trouble will break out. But there is semething coming, and it is not another Peace 'Conference. It may be a new trial t3if strength be- tween Russia and Turkey, or it may be a gigantic conflict between Russia and,Japan for the Corea, or it may be an advance to Pekin. There are cir- cumstances which suggest all these openings, and -Russia obviously wants to make the most of the Present opportunity. Great Britain is engaged in' 'South Africa, and most unlikely to offer any active resistance to slily developed Rx:.ssian plans of aggrandisement. What Trance may do we know Ist. She has her great Exhibition to attend to, and it will absorb all her energies for the time 'being. We may be mistaken as to Russia's desire for war somewhere, but there can be no doubt as to her restlessness and as to the squeezing process she is applying simultaneously at several points.

Cannibalism has always been associated with the uncivilised or the demented famishing, but it appears that popular ideas have not been wholly Correct. The members of a Freach mission which 11„se just arrived from the interior of the French, Soudan report the existence of a cannibalistic nation which, in other respects, has reached a fairly high standard of civilisation. The tribes of the Upper Cavally, we are told, have a high regard for decency. They wear blouses and trousers, Provided by native tailors. :Their roads will bear c...emparison with those constructed by many an Ignglish kcal authocity,and if they were only more accessible to the outer world they might attract some of those cycling touristawho are still hopefully searching for the perfect country. French explorers Were astonished at the intelligence of the natives, the excellence of their tlaroughfares, the dura- bility of their villages, ,and the abundance of, grain and cattle. They were more astonished still when it leaked out that the tribes were canni- hale by preference,and proposed to eat the mission °PPertunity offered, a plan which the French ear.ustrated by departing with all speed. No mis- rtarY seems to have intruided upon the privacy "La Upper Cavally, and unless he went power- .ully armed and with a strong escort it is probable th.at he would never return. Unless reports are rislawding the natives have a language and a Prarattre, the only point upon which they differ ern.civilised countries being the question of cannibalism, in defence of which they are,appar- eratlY, prepared to fight. It ic an odd situation.

div.head: FIRE IT FA.RNWORTH.
div.p: FIRE IT FA.RNWORTH.

Last Saturday afternoon, about 3,30, a man named Webster di-covered that a fire bad broken outquan old unoccupied factory in Farnworth, Widnes. The doors and windows of the lower por- tion of the building, in which there was a large quantity of manure, straw, shavings,' &c., were all ff, and the rubbish had by some means become ignited. An alarm was given, and the Widnes Fire Brigade was summoned. The men, in charge of Foreman Beesley, were soon on the spot, and they ,commenced to play on the burning mass. In about ten minutes, thanks to their well directed efforts, the conflagration was extinguished. The damage was very small, the beams on the floor being only slightly charred. During the h—e-a;Tiog on the river last Saturday utorning, the Rochdale Canal Company's steam flat "Tyne," whilst coming up the river towing another flat, fouled the steamer "Fullvroor of Liverpool. The force of the collision made the flat heel over, cutting through the port aide of the steamer and causing considerable damage, The hands on board thinking the "Fanwood" would go down, and being unable to correctly estimate the extent, of the dam- age.jumped on boarl the flat,and ultimately landed at Runcorn, believing their steamer had sunk. The "Fullwood" however did not, sink, and in ne mean- time steamed from near the Liverpool Landing Stage to opposite Garstnn. where she was subse- quently found and taken in tow by the Garstoa Hopper. The Rev rl.lsarraclongh,deliyered an excellent address on -Ballast ani kind." He said that a ship when going on a voyage with very little cargo generally took ballast to keep the ship safe, and this. though practically vslueless,was very important. This was so with food. Much that was eaten nowadays wassanly ballast, there being no nutriment, in it, and the consequence was im- poverished systems. The drink, many kinds of which were ballast, was not fit nor Advantageous to the system. This remark also applied to reading. Much of the literature that was being read nowa- days was only ballast. whereas gond literature was often despised to the evident decrease of mental culture.. Ac with the br aS and mini, so with the spiritual. 'The existences many wsre living could only be compared to ballast, whilst on the other hand persons embraced the gospel and endeavoured to help others as well as themselves. The quarterly meeting of the above Order was held on Saturday evening, in the Greenway-road School, -under the presidency of Mr. Thomas R Whyte. There was a good attendance of members. After the ordinary business had been transacted, the Chairman,-on behalf of!the division, presented Mr. Themes Cooke with an emblem of merit, which was mounted and framed. It had on it,the follow- ing inscription —"Lifeboat Crew Division. Resolu- tion: That the best thanks of the subordinate divisions be,and are hereby tendered to Bro. Thomas Cooke,fer his valitable services as Worthy Patriarch for two terms. Thos, R. Whyte, patriarch; James Johneon,- financial scribe." The "Chaiiman spoke in appreciative terms of Mr. Cooke, and expressed the pleasure he felt at having to take part in that meeting. Mr. Thomas J Holt seconded the resolution, which was supported by the follow- ing gentlemen :—Messrs. D Bisbrown, -Captain Hindley, Thomas TIOAROM, Samuel Neesom;Samuel Tomlinson, Edward W Key, and James Moores. Mr. Cooke replied, saying that he thanked the members sincerely. and 43hon1d always value the gift. Mr. Thomas 3 Holt, recording scribe, was elected to represent the division at the National 'Division Meeting, to be held in the Drill Hall, Lincoln, on Whit-Monday, JuneAth. VICTORIA-ROAD BOARD SCHOOLS, RUNCORN. An entertainment was given at the above schools onieriday evening with the object of augmenting the•Teachere' Orphan and Benevolent Funds. An interesting programme had been arranged by Mr F Moulton, Miss Kilburn, and the staff, and their efforts were rewarded with a crowded room. Mr. Moulton presided. The programme opened with a pianoforte solo entitled " Blnmenlied," by Master W Williamson. The Standard I. girls gave an amus- ing song described as "Nee Willie Winkle," which proved to be immensely popular with the young folks present. Mr. Brandi followed with the song "'Tin Gee-gee," and Miss Simkin gave an excellent rendering of ," De Old Umbrella;" Miss Newell next recited The Armoured Train," an incident of the Transvaal War. The" Absent-minded Beggar" by Mr Brown. illus- trated (as -most of the songs were) by the limelight wax a distinctly welcome item in the programme and the'boye present sang the chorus with great zest. Mrs lemperley sang "The Flight of Ages,' which was also strikingly illustrated by the lan- tern. Master R Edwards gave a solo on the piano- forte which, bespoke him to be a promising musi- cian. Mr II Branch made his second appearance in the popular" Boys of the Old Brigade." A piano- forte solo, descriptive of the journey to Table Bay, by Mr Vernonowas a capital effort, and fully de- servered the demonstration of applause which fol- lowed. A series of pictures were thrown upon the screen, illustrative of the Transvaal War, and the most recent events in connection therewith. The views were explained by Mr J C Cragg. When these were concluded the following items were rendered ;—" Fiddle and I" and Scarlet and. Blue," by Miss Wood ,; "Fighting Lads of England" Master .1 Wool ; " Awful Little Scrub." Mr Parr; "Rule Britannia;" " soldiers of the Queen," and the National Anthem, which terminated a most successful entertainment

div.head: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.-- RUNCORN IMPROVING.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.-- RUNCORN IMPROVING.
Medical Officer's Annual Report.

Dr. Findlay McDougall, Mndical Officer of Health, for the Runcorn Urban District, has just issued his annual report upon the health of the district, which shows it to be highly satisfactory and an improvement on previous years. We extract the following from his annual report of 1699 :
DIIIINIITTI3N IN FEVER.

To hundred and fifty-nine notifications of infectious diseases were received during the year, as compared with three hundred and eleven for the year 1898, a decrease of 72. Two hundred and eighty-three notifications were received during the year 1897. Twelve cases of scarlet fever were notified, as compared with fourteen for 1898, a decrease of two. Six of the twelve cases oceurred in two houses, and were all imported ; and as for the other s.x cases it was difficult to trace the source of infection. Ninety-eight notifications were received during 1897. Fifty-eight notificatihns of typhoid fever were received during the year, notifying 57 eases, as compared with 24 cases notified during 1898. Thirty- nine houses were affected, one house had four cases, five houses had three cases each, and five houses two oases each. Seventy-four notifications of continued fever were rec3ived during the year,affecting fifty-five houses. Curioeilly enough three of the cases notified were else notified on the same date in April as typhoid fever, they all occurred in one house in the east end of the town, and the remaining number of notifications were received during the felt five months of the year. Fitty-four houses were affected two houses with four cases each, two houses with three cases each, and five with two cases each. Thirty-five notificstions of cantinued fever affecting thirty houses, were received during 1898. Eleven cases of erysipelas were notified during the year. as compared with fifteen eases notified during 1898, a decrease of four; twenty- two cases were notified during 1897. The number of cases of erysipelas notified is decreasing steadily every year. Four cases of membranous croup were notified during the year, as compared with two cases notified during the preceding year, and two cases for the year 1817. Four cases of Puerperal fever were notified, three were netified:ldurieg the preceding veer. Ninety-nine notifications of diphtheria were received during the year a ',elect two hundred and twenty-two received during -1898, and 121 received during 1897, making a total for the three veers of 442. These cover a period of two Years and five months during which the endemic! lasted, 'beginning in the third week in June 1897, and ending with November 1899.
DECREASE IN DEATH RATE.

The number of deaths from all causes registered during the year amnunted to 290, as compared with 331 registered during the preceding year, withirreethe authority's sanitary district. and for the year 1897 of 338 a decrease of 41 over 1898 ,and a deers tee of 48 over 1897. The infant death roll this year does not head the list as formerly. The deaths classified as from 25 to 65 head the list, although the decrease in the infant death list is a small ens, it is satisfactory to find that it is on the decrease. Eighty-nine deaths of infante under one year were registered, and for the year 1898-90 were registered, and for 1897. 108. Over a t ird of thee deaths were registered during the month of August; 45 deaths of one veer and under five were registered, as compared with 59 registered during the preceding year, a decrease of 14, and for the year 1897 a decrease of 26 Thirteen deaths of five and under 15 years were reels- tered. Thirty-four deaths were registered under the same heading during 1898, a decrease of 21, and for the year 1897 a decrease of two. Ten deaths of yt uog per- sons of 15 and under 25 years were registered. Two deaths were registered under the same heading for 1898, and for 1897 15 deaths were registered. Ninety-two deaths of 25 and under 65 years were registered, a slight increase over 1898, the numbers Wing for 1899, 93, and for 1898, 87, and for 1897, 90. Forty cl-attle of persons of sixty-five years and up wards were registered, and for the preceding year fifty-one deathe under the same heading were registerel, and for 1897 forty-one deaths in the same class were registered. It is very gratifying to be able to renort a CONSIDERABLE INCREASE IN THE -LETTING OF EMPTY _ . PROPERTY.

During the year. There iT;Is.o increased and more uniform employment for those that have to toil. The town, if slowly, is gradually aesurning something of its firmer more prosperous condition, and although there may be considerable room for improvement in this direction, still it is satlsfactory to find that the change is on the right side of the ledger. The death-rate is calculated en a considerable increase in the population, which is estimated at nineteen thousand, as at mid- summer, and giving a death-rate for the year of 15-2 per thousand of the estimated population. If the twenty- sue deaths returned under the head of injuries be deducted, the death-rate will be then 14.3 per thousand of the estimated population For the year 1898 the death-rate was estimated at 16 8, and with the addition of deaths frem injuries, the death-rate was increased to 18 per thousand of the estimated population. The authority will observe a very pleasing decrease in the de tth-rate over the previous year. This is the strongest evidence of the keen interest which the authority magi- fr-sts in all matters that concara the improved sanitary coodition of the town, a coodition that compa;e3 very favourably indeed with other ceetve of industry.
DIARItHCE WAS XXCIPTIONALLY PREVALENT

during the month of August. and quite an epidemic ore- "ailed. Owing chiefly to the intense beat of that month. the death-rate was unusually bigh amongst infants and very yeune children. Twenty-seven deaths are certified as due to this cause ; 24 deaths were registered during the month of Augast ; 22 were infants and children under five years of age. Referring to phthisis. Dr. McDougall says :—"This formidable disease is always represented by a varying death list. The year under re- view is crelited with fourteen deaths, and seven are put to the credit of the previous year; 35 deaths were regis- tered RS due to bronchitis, nleuriey, and pneumonia ; 44 from these causes were registered during the preceding year—a decrease of nine; 14 of the deaths were infants and young children under five years of age—a net decrease in the same class, as compared with the previ- ous year of eight. Tie town has continued exceptionally
FREE FROM SCARLET FEVER.

which was regarded at one time as a hardy annual of varying degrees of malignancy. One death was re- ported and twelve cases notified. Six of these were pnrted, and fortunately the outbreak in these instances was confined to the two houses in which it took place. The six other ewe were isolated iastances,with a douht- ful source of infection. The management of this class of cases during the period of infectious activity is getting much better understoeld, and parents are beginning to realise how much they gain by giving heed to the direc- tions of their advisers, not only in the interest of the sufferers, but also in the interest of the community generally. Of memeorannus crnup there were seven deaths and four notifications. Eight deaths have been retnrned as due to enteric fever. Four deaths were registered during the previous year. I think it will be justifiable to take the typhoid and continued fever notifications together; one hundred and thirty-one cases were notified,and as the cases nearly all occurred within a certain area in the same locality, I have no deuht that the caw notified as continued fever had a typhoid origin dor at all events most of them. This locality bad had an unenviable reputation for some years, and has been reported upon before. The sewage soaked condition of the soil and the defective sewerage arrangements are I fear chiefly responsible fer these recurring outbreaks. The Rah and privy pits are in some places so crowded as to make the air malodorous at all times, and the air space has been much encroached upon by all kinds of extraneous structures. I have reason to believe that the moter is receiving the serious attention of the authority, and some drastic remedy cannot be applied a day too seen. When the back passages are receiving attention the sewage-soaked condition of the subsoil should receive attention ale,. Under the heading of "all ether diseases" 151 deaths were returned; seventy under five years, and 81 of five years and upwards. For the previous year one hundred and seventy deaths were registered in the same class, and classified according to age. There is a de- crease for the year of two in the first eleas, and a de- crease of seventeen in the second class. The epidemic of diphtheria which had its origin about midsummer of 1897. continued to about November of 1899, when the lest five cases were notified and no deaths. The number of deaths registered for the first six months of the year amounted to fourteen, and one death occurred in the month of August, making a total for the year of fifteen. July, September, October. and November were free from deaths, giving strong evidence of the mild character of the epidemic. (7g the fifteen deaths thirteen were under end two over fifd years of age Four hundred and forty-two eases occurred during the epidemic Red seventy-six deaths. The rate of mortality is not a high one, but this may be due in a great measure to the character of the disease being much better understood now than formerly. This outbreak ie the only one of its kind that has visited the town fer many years.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.

[BY A CORRESPONDENT.] The Runcorn Ratepayers' Association will, doubt- less, be hoard the last of for some considerable time especially after thu severe defeat of its chosen candidate Ur T Wood. The result of the poll was as I hinted laq week a revelation " Salkeld 272 ; Wood 81." It is interesting to contemplate these figures as showing the influence ef the Ratepayers' Association. It is not too much to suppose that Mr Wood is popular enough to secure 81 votes" upon his own "so that the Association must have an in- finite-imal infitulcice, and the question of "whom de they represeut ?" is now unmistakably and clearly answered.

In elections there are always undercurrents, and if one knows the flow of these subteraneous streams one has a pretty good idea of what is likely or un- likely to happen. The Ratepayers' Association Candidate has either been blind to these little drifts, or utterly indifferent; else he would not have laid his defeat at the door of the Liberal Executive. lie is said to complain of the support he received from the Liberal Community. For the answer to that he should look to himself, for surely no body of Liberals would sell themselves to, or deign to support an Assoe:ation of Ratepayers almost entirely composed of Conservatives.

By the time this appears in print the Runcorn and Widnes Bridge Bill will have passed its third read- ing in the House of Commonw. It only remains to say that the Runcorn Urban District Council have secured clauses for the protection of their rights, and have got almost all they asked for—but I fear that time will show they have not asked for the requisite things, but have rather sought those the least necessary.

A discussion of some length took place at the Urban District Council, on Thursday merning,cou- cerning the overdraft which for years has hung like a mill-stone around the neck of that august body. Row it originated, is quite a mystery, and from the suggestions of members it looks as if none of them knew exactly its true history. One says it was a legacy; and another that it was created by the Council themselves, still another that it was due to an epidemic, and f.o on. But from whatever cause it may have originated, we can all be pretty unanimous about its deletion. As Mr. Imison says "It's gone !" Let us hope it will never return.

As intimated last week someone got scolded for making use of indiscreet utterances—that someone was Mr. Wilson, and between Mr Handley's just indignation, and Mr. Imison's coal chaff, Mr Wilson had an unenviable time. Mr Wilson,however,stuck to his guns and did not apologise, but rather sought to take shelter under the reporter's pencil—charging the dutiful scribes with sins of omission. This is too bid of Mr Wilson, especially after the request —during that memorable speech to that ephemeral Association—that certain of his remarks concerning the Ferry which he gave utterance to, should be allowed to go unrecorded. If the press has been guilty of omission it is rather an omission which would have redounded worse upon Mr. Wilson (on his own confession).

Mr. Stanley Bankes, of Weston, a member of the Cheshire Yeomanry, left Runcorn by the 4.40 train on Tkursday to join his regiment at head— quarters preparatory to sailing for South Africa on the 11th inst. For some days past he has been home on furlough, and his familiar figure sporting a wel 1 fitting suit of khaki has been the subject of much comment. Young Bankes looks quite a mere lad, but the Boers will find him a warm handful for he rides and shoots admirably.

div.p: RURAL RATEPAYERS' MEETINGS.
Frodsh am.

The annual meeting of the ratepayers of Frodeham was held in the Court Room, Main-street, on Thursday evening, Mr. C. E. Linaker in the chair.—The Chairman said it was interesting to mark the progress made in the township during the pest 30 years. In 1869 the ratable value was £7,569, and at the present time £13,279. Th,,, town hid, therefore, practically doubled in importance. He was glad to say that notwith- standing the increased charges upon the township the rates had not greatly increased, and now that a large portion of the loans in respect of the sewerage schemes and water supply had been paid og it might reason- ably be anticipated that the rates vcould be still further decreased. Toe water supply during the past year had paid for itself, although upwards of £4O had been expanded in repairs to one of the pumping engines. He was sure, too, that the parish ihould be very grateful for the £5O from the County Council, a sum which was to be expended solely upon the care and maintenance of the trees planted in Main-street. Ho we also pleasel to remind the alerting of the great improvement executed in Main-street on the north side by the County Council, and he hoped that the south side would be dealt with similarly sometime in the near future. The Footpaths' 'Committee has spent upward of £lB upon the path in Alvanley-terrace and other improvements were in progress upon the path near to Pinmill Brow. (Hear. hear.) Mr. Shore,ehairman of the Lighting Committee.stated that when he first took office there were only 28 street- lamps whereas now there wore 69, and this number was maintained without arc, extra rating. A hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman and Clerk concluded the meet- ing. _ .

div.head: Appleton.
div.p: Appleton.

The annual meeting ni the ratepayers was held in the Appleton Thorne Schools. Mr. John Marsh (chair- man of the Parish Council, presided ever a small attend- Rnc.. The overseers' accounre for the year ending March 25th, 1900, were laid before the meeting. These showed that after all liabilities bad been met a balance of over £4l remained in the hands of the overseers. The Chair- man also explained to the ratepavers present that parish councillors now retained their office for three years, and that there would be no election this year. The meeting closed with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

The Proposed Light Railway. At a meeting of the Little Leigh Parish Council, held in the Schoolroom on Friday evening, when there were present: The Revs. L D Lyon Bennett (chairman), and John Aldis, and Messrs John Mil- lington (vice-chairman), John W Garner, George Moore, John Berton, William Brock, and the clerk (Sydney E Stokes), the following resolution, re Light Railway, was unanimously passed :—" That, the Little Leigh Parish Council regrets that the clause suggested by the syndicate of the proposed light railway is not satisfactory, as it contains no pledge that the western branch shall be carried out as part of the general scheme, and hopes that the defect may yet be remeaied. lint, whilst strongly pretesting against this omission, the council does not deem it wise to oppose the entire scheme." St. Paul's Schools.

The report of the Government inspection of the above schools in religious knowledge, has just been received. It states that the boys' school passed e very creditable examination. Sound and health instruction has been given, and an advance has beet made during the past year. Special praise is due to the lads in standard three. The examination in the girls school commenced with an opening service of hymn and prayer, which were sung and said in a thoroughly orderly and reverent manner. The work of the infants' school has been found in a con- dition of its usual excellence, and the children are reverent at prayer and sang a hymn very nicely. Groups I. and H. were examined together; the children were bright and intelligent; they gave most intelligent answer? to questions based on the meaning of the commandments, and repeated and understood tex's which illustrated simple religious truths. Scripture narratives have been very nicely prepared. Group HI. is the babies' group; they have been taught with sympathy, and were bright and responsive.

div.head: RUNCORN v. BRADFORD.
div.p: RUNCORN v. BRADFORD.
THE THIRD MATCH.
Grand Game at Broughton. RUNCORN VICTORIOUS.

When two teams have to meet three times to decide which is the superior there is naturally a lot of interest manifested in the final encounter, but when, in addition, the teams are the champiens of lAncishire and Yorkshire respectively public excitement becomes intense. This was the position of matters at Broughton yester- day for the fight for the Northern Union Cup, had brought the two champion teams, Runcorn and Bradford together, and each had played on its own ground without coming to a proper decision. The players had been engaged at Runcorn the previous day,but notwithstanding. they were as eager as ever for the fray when they stepped on Wheater's Lower Broughton to make the third time " pay for all." The weather was a bit capricious, sunshine and shower being intermingled, but the ground was in very fair order for the contest, and as the kick- off was not until five o'clock there was a good gate —probably 7,000. Among the number were a good sprinkling of Yorkshiremen. There was a change in each team from the previous day, Cooper re- placing Crompton. and Nixon replacing Jolley. Runcorn again had the good fortune to win the toss a fact which was noted by the crowd. Mr. M'Cutc'eon (Oldham) was tl-le referee and the teams lined oat as follows :

Bradford : Ward,full back ; Green, Cooper, Murgatroyd, and Pollard, three-quarters ; Wood and Prole, half backs; Broadley, Hutt,Barraclough, Neville, RobertFo3, Smayles, Holden. and Feather, forwards.

Runcorn: Houghton, back; Wilkinson, Warder, Butterworth and Jones, three-quarters; Nixon and Faulkner, half backs; Walker, Gayter, Lightfoot, Darlington, Tomlinson, Reece, Taylor and Langley forwards.

Broadley started for the Yorkshiremen and bent in touch. ,tuncorn returned strongly and rushed to the other end, Murgatroyd being grassed. A fine bout of passing cime from both sides, Runcorn be- ing the more dangerous and attacking hotly. But- terworth nearly seo-ed, hilt hesitated on the line and was upset. Wood relieved aicely Houghton sending badly in touch. The men in green started with wonderful dash and Shad all the play to com- mence with. Prole was penalised at 25 line, Houghton failinz frcm a place opposite the goal. Pollard sprinted beautifully down the field to the Runcorn quarter, but the latter were quickly back again. Butterworth got hold and kicked across to Jones, the Bradford men being caught napping. A roar of applause went up as Jones fielded smartly, and raced over at the corner. The first success for the Runcorn men was immensely popular,and "hard lines" was the cry when Houghton hit the post with a grand goal kick. Bradford were slow at heeling out, the Runcorn backs nearly always gain- ing possession. Play was of a brilliant description, the combination on both sides being tip-tip. Butterworth snapped up from the loose and dashing ahead, he gave Jones a fine opening, which the latter again utilised to the full. Houghton was again very near the goal. With Runcorn two tries ahead it seemed all over with the Brad- fordians, who had shown poor fozm up to now. Cooper twice punted badly in touch, and the Linnets scrummaged under the posts. Wood, how- ever, clearbd, and a smart passing run further improved matters, Pollard getting to the centre. Houghton knocked on and Bradford paid their first visit to the Runcorn quarter; They were not here long, and Green had to knock dead to save his side from an )ther cross-kick. Ward fielded clumsily facing the sun and Runcorn scrummaged on the line. Butterworth twice mulled passing—a some- what unusual thing for him. Bradford now began to play with more energy, especially forward, but they did not make much headway. Half-time come with Runcorn still pressing and leading by 2 tries to nil.

Langley restarted and after exchanges J Butter- worth marked coolly. Tne Linnets were the first to attack again, but Bradford showed more dash than before. Nixon mulled and Broadley and Feather dribbled into the Runcorn half. Then Cooper had a drop at goal from half way and was near the mark. Murgatroyd helped by another punt, Houghton being grassed on the line. From a mark by Ward, Cooper tried at goal again a grand attempt falling short. Branford did all the pressing now, but were not so smart as their opponents. Wood intercepted near touch and threw across to his forwards, Feather knock- ing on with a lovely opening. Again Wood was to the fore, and Pollard racing up after a punt collared Houghton over the goal line. Hot work followed,a forward passe poiling Pollard. Runcorn cleared temporarily. Then Prole kicked across and Butter- worth only just got the ball before Cooper. The latter had another try at goal and only lacked force. Next, Wilkinson was penalised for off-side, Cooper landing a goal from a nice position. This event stimulated both sides, and Butterworth made a marvellous mark in the midst of the Bradford men on the line. Shortly after Butterworth suf- fered from a heavy charge by Feather, but resumed. Cooper made a brilliant sprint and tackled Nixon, but all to no avail. Runcorn defended continuously and splendidly, lloughton bringing off a grand save under the pasts. Wood forced himself over but was brought back, great excitement prevailing. Something shady occurred here and Feather was sent off. The next minute Pollard was laid out in mid-field. Very little more happened before the final came, Runcorn winning a splendid game by 2 tries (6 points) to Bradford 1 goal (2 points).
Comments.

The players on boar sides ought to have a whole- some respect for each other by now—and no doubt they have. Two better teams it would be difficult to find anywhere. They were most evenly matched, but there can be no questian that the' wearers of the green' were the better lot Forward and back they were the smarter set, particularly when there was any passing. Now Bradford passed uncom- monly well and accurately, but there was not the rapidity and crispness about their exchanges that there was about the work of the Runcorn backs. Strange to say neither side ahoed any signs of weariness from the hard work of the pre- vious matches, and the game was conducted at a very fast, pace. For the whole of the first half the Linnets quite overplayed their power- ful antagonists, and Jones ran in two pretty tries after fine combination. Bradford seemeri to be waiting for the turn-about as, they livened up wonderfully when they got stri and wind behind them. Then was it Runcorn's turn to defend. And what a defence it was! Time after time the Yorkshiremen seemed bpund to score and on two occasions Houghton and Butterworth staved off absolute disaster by wonderful coolness and certainty in marking. It was a great game, and not for a moment did the in- terest flag. Probably a finer exposition of the ed. BroughtonNorthern Union ground, and !t was a huge treat to the game was never given on the spectators. Coming to individual comperisons, the palm must be given to Houghton and Butterworth, b speedy and ,:a twe tries coal not have been obtained in ber,er style. Forward, Walker was the pick. On the defeated side Pol'ard away the ph lt.ir?t centre on the field. Jones was superbly, the lattpr being far and , and Wood did the beat service, both having liar.). iod.Th of whom luck in not getting substantial reward for their exertions. Ward was overshadowed be his ,is-a-vis, but did not do badly, while Cooper got few chan ,es to shine except in the way of Mott- ning following-up. " Bob " Wood hae put on flash since last he appeared in this district but he is still a strong,resourceful half-back. Only one Yorkshire club now remains in the competition,. and it re- mains for Runcorn to give the County its quietus. Leeds Parish Church will be awkward customers to tackle, but if the Cheshire lads are not too tired this Saturday they should emerge triumphant. And then, what ha for the cup

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
BRUTAL ASSAULT ATI THE WORKHOUSE-A PAUPER
SZNT TO GAOL.

At the Warrington— Felice Court on Saturday before Alderman Wright and other magistrates, Frances Hewitt, last from the Workhouse was charged with cernmitting an aggravated assault on Fanny Birehall, wheel; in the Werkhonse at 10 o'clock the previous enorning.—She pleaded guilty but said that Mrs Birch- all struck her first—Mr. B. Shearer prosecuted on be- 't the Board of Guardians. He said that Mrs. Birc was an assistant to the matron and on Friday moroing was superintending the work in the laundry and wash house. She aeked the prisoner to do a certain thine and she absolutely raft:Bed to do /D. Mrs Birchall went int ; another department and returned shortly af:erwards, whereupon the prisoner assaulted her in a most brutal fashien. She knocked her !down, banged her head on the floor and kicked her, severely bruising her. It took four or five other inmates to pull her away from Mrs. Birchall. The prisoner had been in the Workhouse no lees than 12 times during the last two years. Situations had been found for her but she would not keep them. Whilst she was in the Workhouse she was determined to have her own way. The Guardians kad inetrueed him to press the case. Mrs. Birchen only took up the position of assistant on Mon- day, when she succeeded an old woman who had previ- ously occupied the post. It seemed that as her prede- cessor was an old woman, the inmates had had more of their own way than they should have had. He could not get one to give reliable evidence against the prisoner.— Mrs. Birchall corroborated this statement and denied ever having struck the prisoner,—Dr. raide said he saw hire. Birchall at 3-30 in the afternoon. Her eyes were swollen aed she had evidently been knocked on both eidss of the head as she winced and showed signs of pain when he touched her there. She told him she was bruised en the hip an seemed to be suffering considerable pain. —rrisoner said that Mrs. Shebatl treated her " some- thing cruel" and dared her many a time to hit itter.—Mr. Shearer said that none of the inmates made that accusa- tion against Mrs Birchall.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for two months yr;th hard labour, the magistrates dealing with her leniently on account of it being her first appearance. The maximum sentence was six months.

A LODCIIIII ASSAITLTS HIS LANDLADY. William Fay, a werltnen employed at the Wan ington Corperation Gls Werke appeared before the Borough magistrates on Tussday on a charge of assaulting his landlady, Alice Toppiug, of Longford-street on March 31st. When she stepped into the box to give her evidence her face bore marks of ill-usage and above the left eye there was an ugly wound. The prisoner also seemed to have been in a Way for there were a nunsber of deep scratches disfiguring the face. He had been arrested under a warrant which the magistretes had granted free of crlt, on the previous day. Both parties were repre- sonred by membnrs of the legal profession, Mr Jenkins preseeuting and Mr Browne defending. The ease for the 'proseeution was that on Saturday evening. Mrs. Tepping thinking her two ledgers—Fay and H.rt were in bed, locked up and retired to rest. Shortly aft,r eleven o'clock, the lodgers returned from a neighbouring public-house, and chagrined to find the doors locked, msds a row and demolished a portion of the yard wall. Mrs Topping new put her bead outside the bedroom window and informed her irate lodgers that they had no business to be out at such a time. She eventually came downstairs and opened the front doer. Fay was the first to encounter her and else alleged that he struck her in the face and throw her to the ground. The assault was witnessed by Mr and Mrs Wild,aud they gave corroborative evidence as to the assault.—For the defence, it was denieJ that Fay struck the pleintiff and Hart corroborated this statement. He, however, asbni:ted shaking a few bricks from the wall, but bad since Paid for the damage.—The magistrates thourbt the prisoner might have been aggrieved at being locked out bat that was no juititication for the assault. Fay was fined 10s and costs or 14 days' imprisonnaent,and as an advocate's fee was allowed the fine totalled up to ls ed. The money was paid.

div.p: MINOR CASES.
Warrington Borough Court. FElDAY.—Before Alderman Wright (in the chair), Councillor

Srnethurst, and Dr. Gorn INSANITARY COW SHED —William Owen, 108, Wilderspool- road was summoned for occupying a building as a cow shed without having first made provisions for lighting. ventila- tion, cleansing, water supply, ,on the 12th March.—in- spector Norman -tated that in consequence of information he received he visited the premises in question which were situated in Arpley meadows. There were ten cows in the building which was without proper drainage. The floors were defective and there was no yard of any description. The water supply was obtained from an ordinary pit across the field which was contrary to the Orders of the Board of Agriculture. The „summons was taken out by the orders of tbe Health Committee. The building was ereeted without any plans being submitted.—The defendant said he had occupied the shed for 14 years. At first it was a wooden structure but to make the place warmer he had a brick wall erected. He did not know he had to give notice to authorities. —Dr Goraall remarked that the Health Committee was going to enforce eleauliness and obedience to by-laws and was not going to be influenced by anything but what was right. The defendant shou'd provide for the COW 9 as he did for his children because they were of as much importance as human beings in reference to the supply of milk.—The magistrates decided to adjourn tbecase for a month to give the defendant an opportunity of abating the nuisance. SCENE IN A WORKSHOP.—Mary Dolan and Ann Fogherty, of Rylands Court were summoned for assaulting Sarah O'Hares, 1, Bakehouse-yard on the 22nd March.—Mr. Browne appeared for the complainant. He said she had worked at Mr James Toole's, Feundry-street for 14 years and the defendants were employed at the same place. Mrs. °glares' nephew an t his wife lived with her and last Thursday the nephcw left for South Africa, On the Wednes- day night he went to the totise of Fogherty. As it was his last night at home complainant obj cted to him being away from her house. She sent for him and they had some words. The following day complainant was in the work room at Mr. 'Toole's and Just after dinner Fogherty kept talking stout her sending for the nephew. After having further words with complainant Fogherty left the room and Dolan came in. She had h 0 right in the room. She struck com• plainant in the breast and made use of disgusting language. Several women int.rfered and Fogherty o .me in and struck complainant under the left eye —There was a lack of cor- roborative evidence, so the case was dismissed. THEITB FR3SI THE MARKET.—William Dlcl6o/1. a boy, whose address was given as Pernival's-fold, was charged with stealing from the stall of William Hewitt, in the Market Place at 10.45 on Saturday morning a isomb value d at 4ad. He was further charged wita stealing frem the stall of Da tel Weight at 10 53 on the same morning a bundle of laces value 21c1 and from the stall of Messrs Harks and Spenser at 10.56 a reel of thread, a thimble and a small looking glass value 3d.—He pleaded guilty .—Super- intendendent Moaaghan said that shortly before 11 o'clock on Saturday morning fa.C., Clough was con duty in ,;,.the market in plain clothes and saw prisoner loitering among the stalls in a suspicions manner. He watched him for some time and siw him go to the stall at Mr Wright, take a bundle of laces and put them in his pocket. He arrested him and brought h!m to the Pollee Station and the other articles mentionei in the eharge were found in his possession. Prisoner admitted stealing them and pointed out the stalls from which he had taken them. The boy was a native of Manchester but had run away from home. He could not do any good with him.—The magistrates committed the prisoner to Ard- wick Green Reformatory for live years. DRUNK Dr McCreaney. 3, Jolley-street. was charged with being drunk in charge of two horses and a 'bits in Buttermarket-street at 10.45 on Saturday night.—He pleaded not guilty —P.S. Williamson stated that at the time in question he was on duty at the Police Station. In conse- quence of a complaint he rec dyed ebout the defendant he proceeded to the 'bus terminus in Buttermarket-street. He saw the defendant ' standing on the footpath by a pair of horses attached to a 'bus. The 'bus was turned round ready to go to the Cemetery. The defendant was drunk and utterly unfit to be in charge o! the horses and vehiele. Witness took him into custody and sent P.O.Chrimes for another driver to take charge of the horses. P.C.Chrimes and Newey corrobora- ted.—Mr. J. G. Craik, of Buttermaiket-street, gave evidence to the erect that he was going home on Saturday night and passed the defendant in charge of a 'bus. He was drunk, and witness was afraid that he would fall off the 'bus before he:got to the terminus. He gave information to the police —Defendant denied that he was drunk and called several witnesses.—Joseph Healey, a checker in the employ of Mr. Connor, stat.sd that he saw the defendant at 10.15, and he was then perfectly sober. He did not see him at a quarter to eleven, and defendant could have obtained drink In the meantime.—A Mrs. McKabe and several other witnesses sail defendant was qnite sober.—A fine of 5s was imposed.-- James Green 33, Bostock-street, was on the evidence of P,C. From the evidence it appeared that he entered the watstrman's cabin on the electrical company's works in Horsemarket-street,and not only refused to go away but threatened George Patrick. the watchman—He vets now fined 105 and costs. THEFT FROM THE BARRACIC3. —A SOLDIER SENT TO GAOL. —Rim Burke, of the 3rd South Lancashire Regiment. as charged with stealing from a receiving room in Orford Barracks on Febru ,ry 21st, an overcoat valued at £2 he pro- perty of Harry 13rindle.—He pleaded g .ilty.—He was further charged with stealing by means of a trick from Walter G. Saunders. a sergeant of th , Ist South L ancashire Regiment. the sum of bs on February 28th.—He pleaded not guilty.— Superintendent Monaghan said that the proseautor went to Orford Barracks on the 21st February for the training in the Militia. On entering he left his overcoat in charge of Sergeant Saunders. A few weeks afterwards prosecutor com- pleted his training and went for his overcoat which was found to be missing. Th- prisoner was in the receiving room on the date mentioned and Sergeant Saunders had a conversa- tion with him about the matt,r. He admitted having stolen the overcoat on the same day that it was left in the room. He ha.l gold it to a Mrs. Johnson of Mersey-street for 2s 6d but he told the sergeant that he got ,5s for it and if he would give him Sc he would bring the I coat back again, Sergeant Saunters gave him the Eis and I the prisoner left the Barracks. He returned the same night ' I in a drunken condition having spent the 6s but did not bring the coat.—Evidence was given in support of this statement. —One of the witnesses was Mary Ellen Johnson who said she kept a s.cond-hand shop in Mersey-street. On the 21st February prisoner sold the overcoat at her shop. She gave him Es 6d for it which was all he asked for.—Superiaten- dent Monaghan: Did you think that was the proper value? —Witness : He said he had no further use for it. —Superin- tendent Monaghan: Lid you think that was the proper value ?—Witness : No.—The Snperintehdent : Did you ask him his name and address ? --Witness : No.—The Superin- tendent: Did you ask hint how he got posses- sion of it ?--Witness : He said it was his own.— In answer to the Superintendent witness said it was night time when prisoner brought the coat.—Mr. Bicchall expressed the opinion that action should be taken in cases of that description.—The prisoner said that he borrowed the 5s from Sergeant Saunders so that he might get the cot back by paying double what he received tor it. Unfortunately he could not find the shop and " started gling in one alehouse and another " till he became drunk.— Prisoner was committed to gaol for a month on the first charge. the second charge beine dismissed.—Mrs. Johnson was called forward and told by the Chairman that the Bench was very much dissatisfied with the great number of cases of that description which came before the Court. There was no doubt a kreat deal of laxity on her part, and she would have to be very much more careful than she had been, or she would get into trouble. They would not allow her any costs in the case or the money for the coat, which they ordered to be returned to the owner.

Ald,rmaa Blackburst.

A DINGEROUs PRACTICE. -John Travis, a tramp, who said he had come irorn Manchester, was charrd with sleep- ing in the stable of James Newton, Bruche Farm, Manches- ter-road. at th-es o'clock that roorning.—P.O. Wright stated that at the time in question he was in Manchester-toad when he heard the striking of a match on the premises of Mr. James Newton. He went into the stables and found the prisoner there. He had matches and a pipe in his possession. There was a horse and a large quantity of straw in the stable at the time. The prisoner said he had tramped from Man- chester and wanted somewhere to sleep.—He was committed to gaol for seven days.

THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, APRIL 6, 1900. • PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS. RUGBY FOOTBALL. PRACTICE may not make the lawyer perfect, but enough of it will make him rich. THE man who thinks the wheeling craze will die aut is not quite extinct. THE average man can't help looking worried when his wife and an old sweetheart of his get intimate. HICKS: "Is it true then that you're iiving beyond your station 7 " Wicks: "Yes—two miles." "GFOROE describes the girl he is engaged to as a perfect vision." "Yes, and his sister says she is a sight !" A STATE OF, COLLAPSE.—She: "How did you feel when sea-sick ? " He "Like a punctured tyre." WHEN a man and woman marry, these days, they take each other for better or worse; not necessarily for good. "How do you pairit sunrises? You never Raw one in your life." " That's no drawback. I paint sunsets, and then turn them upside down." "SAY, old man, you are so absent-minded. I believe you are in love." Hobson : "Me ? Oh, ho! ho! ho! Why, don't you know I'm married?" NURSE: "Now, Johnny, go and wash your face and hands before the visitors come." Johnny: "Oh, yes; and then suppose they don't come !" WHEN a young man lays his heart at a young woman's feet, she certainly oughtn't to kick. There is"a good deal of satisfaction to be derived from deciving people who think they 'are deceiving you. APPEAL first to a man's reason, next to his preju- dice, then to his purse, and finally to his vanity. If he is still obdurate, give him up. HEWiTT "You are married, aren't you?" JEwirr : "Well, suppose I am?" I haven't asked Lou your pity, have 1 ? ' iiss swan and the mosquito are not alike in every respect, but they both sing before they die. WHEN we say that a man is not open to argu- ment, it usually means that we couldn't convince him. THE Wife: "What a sweet smile there is on the baby's face, John !" The Husband: "yes, he's probably dreaming that he's keeping me awake." IN THE SAME BOAT.—Friend (on steam yacht) : "I wisn I could afford a steam yacht." The Ow- ner (gloomily) : "I wish I could." PUFFER: "I 'think a good dinner without a cigar is a good dinner thrown away." Mildmay (who can't smoke): "If / smoked a cigar, it would be a good dinner thrown away.' His IDEA.—Tommy Wheels: "It says here 'the common run of humanity.'" Mr. Wheeler: "Well, Tommy ?" Tommy: "I suppose that means ten or fifteen miles." CONUNDRUM (by one who knows) : What is the difference between money and rheumatism? The one Comes slowly and goes quickly, and the other comes quickly and goes slowly. PROVOKING,. INDEED.—" That Charley Porkly is horrid." "Why, dear? I thought you and he Were engaged." "We are, but last night I told him he was too good; for me, and the conceited cox- comb didn't deny it." SWEET Young Lady (in omnibus, to old gentle- man who rises as she enters): Oh, don't get up, please ! I can stencil Old Gentleman: You can please yourself about that, miss ! Pm getting out here. AT HIS MERCY.—Pease: I had an awful time at the dentist's." Hubbard • Worse than you expected?" Pease: "I should say so I He put some of his confounded instruments in my mouth so that I couldn't talk back, and then he told me his bicycle was better than mine." TOOK THE WRONG SHIP.—OId Friend (greeting Mrs. Lakeside, of Chicago, on .her arrival in England) : "Are you not glad to set foot on terra firma?" Mrs. Lakeside: "Terra firma ? Land sakes! I thought this was Southampton." CALLED TO EARTH.—He: "Do you remember when first we met? The dew was on the roses, the air was full of summer scents, and—" She: "Yes ; and now there's no summer, no dew, no roses, and no sense. By the way, have you heard of my engagement?" MRS. CAUSTIC: "John, you are a very clever man— very !" Mr. Caustic (surprised) : "![hank you, my dear; but why do you think so specially?" Mrs. Caustic: "Because you have managed so that I am probably the only one who knows what a fool you really are." PHOTOGRAPHER: "Will you take something to drink?" Sitter: "With pleasure." The photo was taken, and the sitter said, "But what about that little invitation?" Photographer : "Oh, sir, that is just a trade ruse of mine to give a natural and interested expression to the face." MISTAKEN INTENTIONS.—Mies De Richley (an- ticipating): "It is useless, mamma, for Mr. Prosey to come here so often. I can never be more than a sister to him." Mrs. Widow De Richley (dryly) : "I fear, my dear, that it will be impossible for you to be a sister to your mother's second husband." A HARROWING QUESTION.—" SO your rich Uncle Ned has signified a desire to see you. He is pro- bably about to make his will. What are you going to say to him?" "Oh, I'm all at sea about it. I'm afraid that if I tell him I'm doing well, he will leave his money to more needy relatives; and I daren't tell him I'm doing ill, for fear he will leave it to more worthy relatives." • A DIFFICULT SITUATION.—" I'm in a quandary,"' remarked the fire-eating citizen. "Of what nature?" "I challenged that magazine editor." "What did he do about it?" " Sent me a printed .slip saying that my manuscript had been received, and would be read as soon as it could be reached in its turn." DIFFICULT RETROSPECTION.—" My friends," exclaimed the eloquent minister, "were the aver- age man to turn and look himself squarely in the eyes, and ask himself what he really needed most, what would be the first reply suggested to the mind ? " "A rubber neck 1" shouted the precocious urchin in the rear of the room; and, in the con- fusion which followed, the good man lost his place in his manuscript and began again." MRS. TAFAIR (interviewing applicant for posi- tion of "first-class cook ") : "Can you make all kinds of soups, entrées and desserts?" Cook : "Oh, yes'm.' Mrs. ielfair : "Do you make a good mock-turtle soup?" Cook: "Oh, yes'm." Mrs. Telfair (who on account of past experiences is incredulous) : "How do you make it'!" Cook: "Oh, like anyone else does." Mrs. Telfair (per- sistently) : "Give me your recipe." Cook (hesi- tatingly): "Well, I just makes a Loins good soups and then I get:3 the little mock-turtles and I throws 'em in." BACK FROM THE KLONDTKE.—Opening the door in response to an insistent knock, the lady beheld the figure of one.she remembered. "Oh, it is you, is it?" she said icily. "It is I," was the answer, "your long-lost husband, who has come to tell you that he is sorry he ran away two years ago." "Maybe you are sorry you went," retorted the lady, "but I ain't. What did you come back for?" "My dearest, I have been to Klondike, and last summer I accumulated fifty thousand—" " Fif-tss thou-sand pounds ! " shrieked the loving wife as eli-e felt on his neck. "No. Mosquito bites." HIS MALADY.,--" 'eh, tell me, doctor,' ex- claimed the patient's wife, in great agitation, "what is the matter with my husband? He left home but a short tune ago, apparently in perfect health, and a little later burst in and began rush- ing through the house like a madman, pulling this article down, tearing up that one, and overturn- ing the other; trying to pack one thing after another into bundles, or thrusting them into any- thing that wOuld serve as a receptacle. When I strove to find out the cause for his peculiar actions, he answered me in incoherent ejaculations, an finally began jabbering out a lot of outlandish words—names of places I have never heard of— interspersed with mention of vast sums of money and all sorts of nonsensical plans. Then suddenly he threw up his hands and fell down insensible, and has been delirious ever since. "Calm your- self, my dear madam," replied the wise old physician soothingly. "Your husband is Klon- dike& His Mind will resume its normal sway as soon as he finds out that he cannot borrow the five hundred dollars necessary for the purchase of an 4:Pita. In tlge meantime I will administer this opiate, and when he awakes and has visited hie friends he will soon be himself again."
