NORTHERN UNION CUP COMPETITION. THIRD ROUND.
Rochdale Hornets Defeat Warrington.

The "Ihird round of th. 3 Cup Competition brought Warrington and Rochdale Hornets together on the ground of the latter, an Saturday. There was a large rate, about 7,000 people assembling to watch what was Expected to be a close contest. Warrington brought nearly a thousand supporters with ttem, and they he!ped to moll the numbers. The weather was as good as could be wished, but the state of the ground was abo- minable. There wai quite two inches of thick mud on the greater portion of the playing p:ttch,and the Hornets officials had not made it any bett r by spreading saw- dust on the surface. There was lot of dissatisfaction felt on the Warrington side. Mr. Robinson of Manning- ham, was the referee, and the teams turned out as selected. ' •

Warrington : Hallam, full back ; Fish. Isherwood, Hockenhall and Jones, threequarters ;;Bate and Burgess, half backs ; Taylor, Thardruan, Morrison, Eden, Mere- weathei, Scholtze, Swift, and Antrobus, forwards.' Roohdale Hornets : Platt, full back; Wightmari,Rigg, Hickey, and Martin, tbreequarters ; Kruger and. Allen, half backs; Ashworth, Harrison, Hodgkinson,Langhorn, Trembath, Wood, Wilson, and Cooper,forwards. Harrison started for the Hornets and exchange kick- ing followed, the advantage, eventually resting with Warrington. Bate got hold and kicked across to Fish's wing, but the ball roiled in touch. More long kicking. followed, Taylor marking and sending to Platt who was tackled on the line by Morrison. Warrington now appeared to have a chance of scoring, but Bate was penalised and the Hornets punted clear, Warrington kept in the home half, but correct football was impossible on such a ground, play being of a scrambling nature. A charge down by Rigg sent the ball into the Warring- ton half, where tbe Hornets gave some trouble, the for- wards playing particularly strongly. Fish sent them blck by a fine punt, Eden upsetting Platt again near the line. Warrington heeled out and the ball was Passed to Is.horwood, who threw firwa.rd and lost a fine open- ing. A fine rush by the home forwards beat the War. rington backs. Hockenhall fell in trying to save, and the ball was rushed over the line, but the score was disallowed for off-side. Half-time came with no score. _ _

Taylor restarted, and ekrly on Rigg secured and dropped, the ball passing outside the posts, by a mere trifle. The heavy ground seemed to be telling on War- rington, and they were pressed back persistently. good defensive tactics were shown however, one or two pass- ing movements helping to raise the siege. The ball was bad to handle however, and Fish never got a decent chance on the left. Warrington attacked for a time, Jones dribbling half the length of the field only to be obstructed when he had the line at his mercy. Another penalty against Warrington drove them back, the referee seeming to have a hazy notion of the 5 yards' rule. Rigg had a penalty shot, but failed, Then Kruger passed back to him in nice position, but Isherwood was on the alert and pre- vented Rigg dropping. Even play followed, Rigg kick- ing down the field. Efallarn mulled for the first time, and Wight:elan racing up scored a somewhat lucky try. There was no goal. Warington now roused up and made a dash for the line, but the fine kicking of the Hornets' backs kept them at bay. Isherwood gave Fish a nice pass, and the wing man made a great effort, but wes stopped by Meg and Platt after a long run. War- rington were gradually pressed back, and the end came I with the Hornets winners by a try to nil.

div.head: Runcorn v. Bradford.
div.p: Runcorn v. Bradford.

A crowd of about 4,500 people assembled at Dwell-lane on Wednesday, to see the replayed tie between the champions of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Sections, in the struggle for the Northern Union Cup. The match was brimful of incid-nt and excitement, and in the re- sult proved indicisive, as both teams scored a try. The teams faced as under : —Runcorn. Houghton, back ; Wilkinson, Warder, J Butterworth, and Jones, three-quarters ; J Faulkner and J.. Jolley, halves ; S Walker, F Gayter, A Lightfoot, Alf Taylor, Reece, Tom- linson, Langley, and Darlington, forwards. Bradford : Ward, back ; Crompton, Green, Pollard, 'and F Murgatroyd, three-quarters ; Wood, Prole, halves; Breadley, Hutt, Berraclough, Wright, Grayson, Laidlow Holden. and Feather, forwards. Mr. Priestly, Broughton, was the referee. Broadley commenced for Bradford,against both sun and wind; Wilkinson return d,and from a scrummage near the centre, Jolley initiated some beautiful paseing.Faulkner, Butterworth, Wilkinson, Lightfoot and Jones raking part. Shortly alter, Ward tcuched down. Hutt was , cautioned tor heav,ly obstructing Warder. Butterworth I got an opening and passed to Faulkner. The latter, however, stumbled at a critical stage. Runcorn then , had the best of affairs. Broadley was conapicious for a breakaway,and Murgatroyd further improved. Pollard getting a chance carried ehe game from Bradford's half and Houghton had to save,clearing with a rush. Hough- ton followed up grandly and put in a superb run. Being collared, he loosed out the ball, and Warder picking up scored a fine try. Jolley kicked for goal, but was wide. Bradford got away with a rush which Gayter saved nicely. Ward knocking-on gave Runcorn a further chance, and a drop by Jolley just missed by inches. Gayter got cautioned for shady practices. A succession of mai ks followed. Then Pollard got an opening and was off only to be brought to grass by Jolley and Wilkinson. Bradford looked line scoring,but a previous knock on brought them back. Murgatroyd put in a beautiful run shortly afterwards, and a stay was made in the Runcorn half. Good defensive play, however, on the part of Butterworth and Houghton kept the home line intact. Houghton kicked dead. A free kirk gave Runcorn relief,but Bradford were back again. The tackling was very keen, and occasionally developed roughly. Gayter was again cautioned for heavy tackling'. Runcorn got a good position on the Bradford line. Bradford got possession twice or three times, but failed to improVe on account of the fine play of the Run- corn team. Nice passing by the Bradford backs was frustrated by Hought'on, who got heavily pushed into touch. Big kicking followed, and the Bradford back found touch a'conveniedt relief on several occasions. Half-time arrivedi—Rtiticorn, 1 try (3 points) ; Bradford, nil. Taylor kicked off for Runcorn upon resuming, and at once Bradford visited the Runeorn line. Houghton spoilt Jones from effecting a fine mark. Going strongly, Bradford continued to press. Houghton saved several times. Butterveorth gained further relief with a mark, but as good an effort on the part of one of the Bradford forwards-rkei6ed no recognition. Runcorn with a suc- cession of brilliant rushes then got a footing in the Bradford twenty-five, but did not stay long. Pollard put In a fine dash, the result 'of good passing, and almost succeeded in scoring. Off-side against Bradford again transferred the venue. But once again Bradford re- turned to the attack. Butterworth was held opposite the posts. Wood took a penalty kick, but failed. The running WAS then taken up by Crompton and Murga- troyd ; Warder, Butterworth and Jolley responded. Each end was visited in turn, and once Houghton was compelled to touch down under his own sticks. Brad- ford continued to press and though they fairly penned therLinnets, owing to lack of finish they could not score. Ward hazarded a drop, which went inside. Several smart interchanges followed, and as a result Bradford were awarded another free kick. Wood played grandly, and was well backed up by Pollard. Hough- ton, however, marked and relieved. Runcorn gained relief and appeared to be holding a strong position, but a slight looseness On the part of Jolley and Wilkinson gave Green an opening. Be took it and passing out to Pollard that player ran in a superb try, just on time. Holden tried to convert but miserably failed.—The final result was :—Runcorn, 1 try (3 points); Bradford, 1 try (3 points).

div.p: Runcorn Petty Sessions.
MONDAY. —Before ltesirs. Henry lksynords (presiding)
and F. J. Norman.

A YouneFue. FonTBILL 13NTEUSLAST.—One way of getting to see the loetb :11 match b deveee Bradford and Runcorn, which at any rite bad the appearance of ingenuity, was that adopted by John Kelly, aged 16, son of Mrs. Kelly, 13, Brunswick-street, Runcorn. It appears the led took three cotton shirts, an wore a pillow case, and a shawl, valued at about 9e from the house, and pawned theea utilising the proceeds(2s 3d) to pay his fare to Bradford,and see the match. He succeeded ; hut was not A itt le surprised upon his retur home, on Saturday night, to fial Constable Bowyer waiting to conduct him to the Poll ie Station.—Missing the articles, the mother had given information to the police, and the re- eult of a few visits to the'locet pawn shops revealed the fact that the property had been divided area pawaed by the boy, three shirts, an xprou and e pillow sl!p bring disposed of at Dodd's, for Is 9d ; ant the shawl. at Lign,fax,s. for 81 —The mother told the Bench sue did not wish to press the charge, as, at the time she give information to the pulse she was net aware it was her own sou who bed taken the articles. The boy had never te-em guilty of anything of that nature before, and had been a good lad te her.—The Chairman said the offence Was too serious to be overlooked altogether, and bound prisoner over in one surety of i 5 to come up for judgment when called upon . Tna aseeneetteoe DucK-seoere " ax-Punete THOROUGH- FARES.—The following youths: Harry Ainsworth. Frederick Wood. Joseph 4 ewton, Alfred Rllford, Arthur Lightfoot and Walter Joinson, all of the neighbourhood of Chaucer-street, were summoned for throwing stones in the public street on the 23rd of March —They pleaded not guilty.—Constable Bowyer swore to seeing all the defendants playing at "Duck- stone " in, company with lots of smaller boys in Chaucer- street. He captured them, but only the elder boys bad been proceeded against. Numerous complaints had been received about the boys, and considerable damage had been done to the brick-work against which the boys dashed their stones. A large number of windows in the vicinity bad at o been damaged, but, he did not lay the latter charge against the preset defendants.--Eliford denied that he was playing.— Thp Bench considered that all the boys were playing the dangerous game, and they would have to pay the costs 4s 6 as a warming. DRUNK KNEE E.—Thomas Atherton,Hallvfood Farm ,Halton pleaded guilty to being drunk, at 11.30 p.m. on the 25th March, and was fined be. STEALING FROM A. BEaRHOUSE AT RUNCORN.—Maggie Staunton, and Martin Starkey, of Water-street, were charged with feloniously stealing two gallon') of beer, valued at 3s, the goods of Messrs. Greenlet Whitley and Co.. at Runcorn, on the 24th of Nlarch, 1900.—The female d efendant did not appear, and a warrant was issued against her, —Starkey pleaded not guilty.—Hugh Starkey, aged 12, residing with his mother, at 4, Water-street, swore he was a brother of the the defendant. About 2 o'clock on Saturday last, he went to the " Rose and Shamrock " beerhouse, in Mersey-street, in company with M igeis etaunten He get in at a window in the back yard; and opened the back door for Staunton, by withdrawing the bolt On going inside, Staunton entered the cellar, and tried the beer taps, until she came to a barrel from which she succeeded in drawing beer. His brother was not there on hat occasion, but came with them the following day (Sunday). when practically tbe same course was followed. The beer was taken home and drunk by 'Maggie Staunton, and witness's mother, They tel ) the mother that they had bought the beer. The stone bottle pro- duced was one they got from Sam Houghton's. Maggie Staunton had filled it with beer. Witness's mother was a widow, but Maggie Staunton was a married woman and lived with th m —By the Bench: He knew he had no business in the house, and that they were stealing. —Con- stable John McLeod deposed, to getting information which caused him to get the assistance of three other constables to watch the place, which ultimately resulted in the arrest of prisoners. The last witness had made a statement to him in the preserve of both defendants that " Maggie Staunton and the accused had takes the beer."— Frederick Pearson. cashier in the employ of Messrs. Greenall Whitley and Co., of Wilderspeol, intimated. on behalf of the company, that they did not wish to press the charge. They only proceeded in the matter to show they would not allow sueh things to take place. The " house" was a beer-house, stud had been tenantless for about two months.--Defendant said he was not guilty. He had certainly been to the house, but did not take the beer—The Bench were of opinion that defendant must have been aware that he was doing wrong, and imposed a five of 10s oe 7 days with hard labour. A DRUNKARD HEAVILY FINED. -John Keen. of Runcorn, for being drume and disorderly on-the 31st of March, and let of April respectively, was- fined 5s and 8s 6d sects, and be and 6s costs. or 14 days with hard labour —The fines were paid.

div.head: "AND WHEN THE EVENING WAS COME, HE WAS THERE ALON E."—(Matt.)
div.p: "AND WHEN THE EVENING WAS COME, HE WAS THERE ALON E."—(Matt.)

Where'er He journeyed day by day, What wonders marked the wondrous way Of Him who came the world to save: The sick He healed, the hungry fed, To rest and peace the weary led, And raised a loved one from the grave. Nor was this all: when night drew on, And home the wond'ring crowds had gone, He sought the moutitain's peaceful shade : Ani there, unseen, while others slept, "The Man of sorrows "vigil kept, And for the poor and sinful prayed. And now, perchance, the mild gazelle May roam where soft His footsteps fell, Far from the beaten paths of men: And stars of heavenly ray serene Still nightly cheer the desert scene That formed the Saviour's temple then. But 0, Thou blessed Son of God, We may not tread where Thou hast trod, Nor kneel where Thou hash knelt in prayer: 'Tis only ours in dreams to trace Thy lonely path and holy place, And fancy what Thy pleadings were. Yet still the eye of faith would rise Far, far beyond the distant skies, And see Thee on Thy glorious throne ; The same sure friend of want and woe As when Thou liv'dst with men below, And made their sorrows all Thine own. J. H. W. CLINDINNING.

Warrington County Petty Sessions 10. UR LOCAL CHURCHES. Professor Drummond at Cairo-street Chapel. The Rev. Principal Drummond, LL.D., Lilt. D., of Oxford (father of the Rev. W. H. Drummond, pastor), occupied the pulpit at the above chapel at the morning and evening services last Sunday. 1,4 the morning Dr. Drummond preached an able discourse from the words : —" He that spared not His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all, how shall He not with Him also freely give us all things ?" Romans viii. 32. Gospel Hall.

WINDOW SMASHING AT BURTONWOOD.—SamueI Hall WAS summoned for ccrumitting damage to a window In the "Elm Tree!' Inn. On Sunday April ist the preacher was Mr. D. Williams of Manchester, the subject of his address being the story of Rebecca's Choice from Gen. 24. In Abraham send- ing his servant a loag jlurnel to find a suitable bride for his son 'mac, we have a beautiful picture of God sending forth his servants into the world to win souls who are to form the Church, the bride of Christ. Each person who hears the Gospel invitation is responsible to God and either accepts or rejects the invitation. Rebecca's heart was won by the glowing description the servant gave of Isaac and A braham and her choice was "1 will go." How diff-rent to the choice of the father-in-law o Moses who was invited to join in with the Israelites and share their blessings but he said " I will not go."

Drownin Fatality at Bewsey.

In the Parade let) .ra at the Police Station at noon on Tuesday, Mr, Br;Oouse conducted an inquest,on the body of Thomas Billington, puddler, (45); of 31, ICatherine-street, which was found in the S. Helens and Sankey Canal at Bewsey on Saturday evening. Hannah Billington, wife of the deceased. said that during the last eig-,t weeks he had been suffering from influenza; and had frequently complained of pains in his head. At 8.30 on Saturday evening she went out, leaving the deceased by hitr.self in the kitchen. About an hour afterwards, on her return, she found that he had gone out, and he was brought home dead at midnight.-L-Jsmes Billington son of the deceased, stated that at nine o'clock on Satur- day evening he was in Catherine-street when he saw his father walking in the direction of the town. He spoke to him, but he did not answer.—Thomas Moody, a forge labourer, of 46, Pierpoint-street, said at 9.45 on Saturday evening he and some friends were on the canal bank at Bewsey,when they heard a splash in the water. They hurried to the spot and saw. the deceased struggling in the middle of the canal. The Preservation of Local Documents.

Sir,—Will you kindly alaw throwzh the medium of the " Wsrrington Examicler " to i:M;ir:Ll9 upon all whom it may concern, the desirability of search:ng for, and preserving any bo.ks or papri, printed or written, that relate in any way to the past h;story ot W-,trington and district, and the doings or its farmat inhabitants. The Treasury, recognising the importance of preservirs•%, local documents, has recently instituted an engoify as to their wlacreabouts and accessibility, it is an opportune time then ta call attention to the subject, so far as our town and dis- trict is concerned. Much important matter might be brought to light, if a thorough search were made, which in all probability is new slowly perishing through dust, damp, and other destructive agencies. Many valuable documents have, no doubt, in the past undergone more certain destruction, by fire or the paper mill. Let us preserve what may remain ; it is not only desirable to do so, it is a du-y we owe to posterity. The following are some of the records pertaining to the past history of a parish or township : (1). Pariah registers, churchwardens' accounts, enclosure award, anl tithe commutation maps, and other church docurnants: These are, or ought to be in the parish chest or safe. (2). Records of the Court Rama and Court Leet, Borough Court records, constables' accounts, overseers' assessments, Freemen's rolls, poll books, coroners' rolls, apprentices' indentures, minute books, non-parochial r-gisterg, school registers, etc. Th..! descendants of former officials may possibly possess books or papers of this class. . . .

Besidee the two classes of documents just mentioned, and which are really of an cfEciel nature, there should exist a great variety of mater of a miscellaneous character, all ef imporeanee and :•,o the student of local history :—Broadsides, prints and drawings, pies of estates, old leases, societiss' reports, extracts from parish and other register, docaments of any kind con. teirsing lists of namee,or referencee to places and events, loy,ters ; family memoranda, etc. Many persons will have miscellanea of this kind, which (except private matter) wou!d be oehanc el in vale if eentrelied in one gene .al collection. A uo:ed writer on local hietory says "Every scrap of pe per of paq genee etions, showing the inner working of par3chial life, peeeesses some hietory of its own ; and future geaerations will thank us for their preservation. The Treasury, in its schedule of enquiry, asks for suegestions as to appropriate Local Centres, and suit- able custodians, for tee future preservatien, arrange* =int and study of these local records. So far as Warrington and district is concerned, the most suitable depository is, unquestionably, the Municipal Museum. This institution already possesses a remarkably fine eel. lention of local books aed documents carefully preserved and arranged. It is therefore expedient that other local documents either known at present, or discovered here- alter,shcutd be added to those at the Museum, and time auement a collection,the value of which cannot be over estimated.—Yours faithfully.
JOHN W. HOWAHTEI
Stockton Haath, 3rd April, 1900.

div.head: ALLEGED ROBBERIES AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: THE ALLEGED ROBBERIES AT EARLESTOWN.
PRISONER COMMITTED FOR TRIAL.
Remarkable Case.

At the Warr'aagton Occasional Court on Tuesday afternoon, before Mr. F. A. Frost, Agnes Hudson, a yoang woman employed at the " Oddfellows' Arms," Earlestown, was charged on remand with stealing from her employer James Lythgoe, a cash bag, five sugar crusbers,one pint bottle of whiskey, and one pint bottle ot rum, ot the value of 7s 6d. and £42 6s lid in money some time between July 1899 and the 16th March, 1900. —Mr J W Knowles who prosecuted,said that the prisoner came into Mr Lythgoe's employ in July of last year. At that time her wardrobe was not by any means extensive in fact her dress seas rather plain for a girl in her degree of life. She was engaged in the capacity of servant and to assist at the bar. Two or three days after her arrival she told a Mrs Roberts, a char- woman to take her halts to he repaired. She said she was not in a positicu to pay for the repairs until she got her first month's wages. Mrs Roberts took the boots and on the following day the pris- oner gave her the money to pay tor the repairs. Her wages were 22s a month. In the following October the prisoner went to Liverpool and pur- chased a very stylish hat, an extraordinary one for a girl in her position. She purchased it at Messrs. Templeton's and Co's. Loadon-road and paid 30s for it. Curious to say she paid all the money in silver. In March this year she went to the shop of Owen Owens in London-road and purchased a jacket for which she paid £2 17s 6d. She was serv3d by a young lady named Hilda Fitzgerald. She paid for the jacket in silver, in shillings with the odd sixpence in silver. She also asked the young lady in the shop to give her a sovereign for twenty more shillings, which was given to her. In eonsequence of prisoner having the fancy bat and jacket and money being regularly missed from the till suspicion was cast upon her. The prosecutor's son Thomas Lythgoe who managed the house bad missed money on several occasions and a Miss Edwards who anted as house-keeper and as4isted at the bar had also found money to be missing. Th? police were called in on the 16th March and zlergeant Lings searched the prisoner's boxes,and found in them a cash bag,five sugar crushers, a pint bottle of whisky, a pint boatel! of rum and £42 63 lid in money. When charged by Sergeant Lingo the prisoner replied "I did not take all the money. I had some when I tame." He (Mr. Knowles) asked the magistrate to commit her tor trial to the Liver- pool Quarter Sessions. The prisoner said that she did not take all the money which was an admission that she took some of it how much she did not say—Evidence was then called the first witness being Thomas Lvthgoe, who managed the business on behalf his father—Ellen Roberts. a char- woman of 20,Regent-street,Earlestown stated that when the prisoner toid her to take her shoes to be mended she said she was "spent up." Witness advised her to ask Miss Edwards, the housekeeper to advance her some money before her month was up. 03 the following day prisoner gave her the money to pay for the repairs, this being More the end of her first month.—Charles Halstead Dudney, the manager for Messrs. Templeton and Co., gave evidence as to the prisoner buying the hat produced on the 19th October, 1899.—Eliza Edwards the house- keeper for James Lychgoe, said she did not advance the prisoner any wages during, her firsts month of service. She did not ask for any—Hilda Fitzgerald, sales woman, at Messrs. Owen. Owens, said the prisoner bought the jacket produced fer £2 17s. 61. She paid for it in shillings with the odd 61 Witness noticed that she had a considerable number of shillings left and suggested that she should change twenty of them fora sovereign. The prisoner did so.—Sergeant Lings said he apprehended the prisoner at 2.30 oa the 16th March at the Oddfellows' Arms, Earlestown. He asked her to show him her bexes as he intended to search them. He went with her to her bedroom and she unlocked her boxes and handed to him the cash bag produced coataining money, five sugar crusheis, the two pint bottles of whisky and rum respectively and . another bag with money in In one box there was a small china ornament containing 293 in 3d pieces. The money totalled to £42 6s 11d. He charged prisoner and she replied" I did not take all the money. I had some when I came." Prisoner, who had n?thing to say and did not cross-examine any of the witnesses was com- mitted fer trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions.— Prisoner was then charged with stealing, some time between July 1899 and March 16:1 1900, a gold breast- pin, valued at £1 ls,the property of Thomas LythgGe.— Mr. Knowles said that when P.S. Lines searched the prisoner's box the breastpin was also found. Tne prisoner turned to Mr.Lythgoe and said, "That is yours, Tom, I took it from your drawer." Evidence having been given by Thomas Lythgoe and Sergeant Ling', the prisoner was committed to the Smsions on this charge als ).

On Satur lay night a woman named Jane Elorabin .53 years of age,wife qf Charles W Horabin met with an accident which unfortunately terminated-fatally. Betweea 11 and 12 o'clock she was carrying. a child upstairs to had, when her husban I w:to vv,s ia the kitchen heard her fall, and hurrying to the stairs fould he lying a", the bottom with the child under- neath her. Dr. Watkins was immediately called in and he attended her until her death which took place next day, the case being hopeless from the first, as the woman had dislocated her neck. ACCIDENT AT EARLESTOWN. On Friday afternoon a boy named James Forshal living at St. Helens, and working for Messrs. Tickle, contractors of St. Helens, at the new Tower which is being en4cted in ceneection with Sc. Peter's Church, Newton, accidentally fell from a scaffold, a distance of about 23 feet. He came in contact with a wheelbirrow and was badly injured about the head. He was removed to St. Helens, and received as an inmate of the hospital there, where it was found that he had received serious internal injuries, and he now lies in a precarious coalition attended by Dr. Jackson. div.head: CLUB.
div.p: CLUB.

The annual geaeral meeting of the members of this club was held in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, Earlestown on Monday evening. Mr W. Harrison presided ant there was a fair attendance of members. The Secretary (Mr E J Mullins) submitted his report on the oast season's working, which showed that tee club had 17 fix- tures, 11 of which teey played. Oat oi: these they won 3, lost 6, drew 1, and 1 was a tie. They had scored 647 runs for the loss of 100 wickets, against their opponents 687 runs for 104 wickets. The state- ment of accounts showe I the club to be in a good financial condition. The election of officers was proceeded witb,and resulted as follows : President, Rev E W Bocock ; vice-presidents, Messrs E J George and T Ormand ; treasurer, Mr W Jones; secretary, Mr EJW 1 ullins; captain, Mr IV Morris; vice-captain, Mr G Taylor ; committee, Messrs Vir Harrison, W Morse, A Harrison, G Taylor, J T Austin,J H Woods. The club has become affiliated to the St. Helens and District Amateur Cricket League.
A Minister's Conscientious Objection.

On Wednesday, at the Borough Police Court the Rev. J. T. Schofield made an application to the magistrates, Messrs. Geddes (in the chair) and Birchall for a certificate exempting his child from vaccination.—The Chairman : Why do you claim ext-nption ?—Applicant: I b6iieve vaccination would be injurious to his hltilth. I have a con- scientious objection to vaccination. The Chairman : You have no regard for other people.—Applicant : Certainly. If is because I do not believe in vaccina- tion. It I thought it was beneficial to other people I should have the child vaccinatel—The tion was granted, the ChairrnAu remarkimg that it was really against the wish of the Bench to grant these certificates.
Brick-street Church Independent Methodist Band of Hope.

The sixth entertainment given in the schoolroom on Tuesday evening under the presidency of Mr. E. Lloyd Jones (secretary of the Warrington and Dis- trict Band of Hope Union) pro7ed very entertaining and instructive,every item of the programme pe.sing off well. There was a good attendance. The Chair- man, who was listened to very attentively, gave a spirited address on the work of the temperance movement, and spoke on the strength of moral courage required to resist temptation,and of speak- ing out boldly our convictions relative to the evils of intemperance. The following recited :—Slissell Ethel Bibby, Clara Wilson, Polly Higham, Florry Wilson, Jenny Bennett, Polly Taylor, and Master Thomas Gallop. The Juvenile Choir gave a choruS entitled "The children are gathering from far." The songs" Ring the bell watchman," and 'The Min- strel Boy" were rendered in a creditable manner by Miss Cissy Holt, as was "Beautiful Home " by Mist; Elizabeth Gallop The following dialogues "To the Rescue,"" Husband and Wife," "Women's Rights," and "Circumstantial Evideace," which depicted. good morals, were satisfactorily gone through. A hearty Tote of thanks was accorded to the chairman for his Services, which were suitably responded to. The doxology brought to a close an enjoyable meet' ing.

div.head: EATESF NEWS.
div.p: EATESF NEWS.
The Attempted Assassination of the Prirce of Wales.
BRUSSELS, THURSDAY.

People last night could talk of nothing but the attempt on the life of the Prince of Wale, and ex- pressions of indignation were heard on all sides. Sipido,in examination,said the ambitions of those who by letting war loose were sacrificing so many human lives deserved to be punished. When he saw the Prince of Wales was going to pass through Brussels be decided to make himself the avenger of humanity and kill the assassin. He regretted his plan failed. The magistrates are convinced Sipido desired to screen someone else. Sipido's parents were deeply affected when they heard what thei son had done, " What disgrace to us," the motaer sobbed. "We have always worked to bring up our children properly. It can't be true what you tell me. He has never had a revolver." The father said, "On Sunday I gave him two francs. If he has done what you say he deserves to be guillo- tined."

div.head: Queen and the Outrage.
div.p: The Queen and the Outrage.

It goes without saying that the lamentable attack on the Prince of Wales in Brussels formed the sub- ject of much inquiry and solicitude from the Vice- Regal Lodge, Dublin. Reliable informltion has been obtained which goes .to show that the Queen was not given any causa for alarm. The news was conveyed to Her Majesty with becoming gentleneps and discretion, and she was further reassured by a telegram direct from the Prince himself, in which His Royal Rigidness treated the matter very lightly Death of the Hero of Plevna. CONSTANTINOPLE, THURSDAY.
Ghazi Osmau Pacha, the hero of the defence of Plevna who had been confined to'his bed for some time, bet whose condition subsequently showed some improvement, died last night.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
Good News from Mafeking.

Lourenco Marquee, Wednesday, 4.15 p.m.—Defi- nite news has reached here that Colonel Plumer made a dash towards Zeerust on the 25th. The natives however gave timely warnin„; to the Boer commando there, and they precipitately retreated. Colonel Plumer's party came within slund of the Boer guns bombarding Mafeking. They met with no opposition: There is a strong belief that he will yet be able to effect the relief of the beleaguered garrison.
South Lancashires Rushing the Boers Before Ladysmith. Letter from a St. Helens Man.

Mrs. Hart, of Lathom-stnet, Se Helens. has received the following letter from lux son, 2724 Priv ate Jamcs Bart, of the lit South Lancanhire, who took part in the fighting and triumphal entry into Ladysmith : Ladysmith, March 3.—Dear Mother,— We have had some awful times here since I wrote to you, but thank God we have come through it all safe and victoriou3. I suppose you will have heard about our regiment rushing the Boers and ae lievi ng Ledy9mi ch. Although our regiment made a mistake it came out all right. We were ordered by the general to cherge the hill on the right, and the men rushed off with fixed bayonets, with- out receiving the order proper. We cleared the hill on the right and the left and the valley between. All the other regiments cave U 3 a great cheering for it, and when We were marching through Ladysmith the cheer- ing for the South Lenceshires was awful. lam glad we have relieved these poor fellows. They are nothing but living skeletons, and they may well be, for their daily fare consisted of 4eizs. of biscuits and 3 )zs of tneelies (Indian corn), so you rev guess how the poor fellows felt. When they saw U 9 they were ready to cry with deligkt. I see by the papers that they say that the Boer is a brave, plucky fellow. If he is I know where there are plenty. They cannot fight when you get them on equal terms, and they evee have their wives with them loading their rifles. You cam see any amount of women here as well as men. Sam Purcell was shot through the thigh on Thursday, and there were three from St. Helens killed. Higgins is in hospital with dysentevy.

div.head: Storming of Pieter's Hill. A South Lancashire's Description.
div.p: The Storming of Pieter's Hill. A South Lancashire's Description.

Writing to his parents who reside at 4, Da Warrington, Lance-Corporal A. Quinn, "A" Company of the Ist South Lancashire Regiment says :—"We left Claieveley for Colenso on the morning of the 14th Febru- ary and were very early engaged as the Bo3rs were on all the surrounding hills. We stopped on a small bill called Hussar Hil for a few days whilst our naval guns were shelling the enemy's trenches. We crossed the river Tugela after we had driven the Boers from our side and on the 26th we were in the firing line. We had to advance under a very heavy rifle fire from the Boers who were on the hill tops. We took the bills and Sir Charles Warren as we left was saying "Look at them (the Leneashires)." We faced the music alright, our Company being in the front with the Colonel, and other Companies 50 yards in the rear. We did everything that was expected and sto,..iped on the small hill for the next two days firing at the Boers. I used about 1,500 ronnds myself. You cannot tell how many you hit. We were relieved from our position by another regiment, the West Yorkshire. We retired across the river and had two days' rest for the good work we had done. We started again on the morning of the 28th February. Each man had 200 rounds of am- munition and;it beiog the anniversary of the day we lost Majuba Hill everybody was determined to get their own back. We were " lying in between a couple of regi- ments but more to the rear. Our Colonel said the Boers were enfilading the West Yorks so he brought us right in front of them. We were in the valley and right under the fire from three hills and we fired about 60 rounds at them. Our Colonel gave the command to cease firing and fix bayonets and said "Come en my men. Let us charge on them." We were all off like lightning. We never thought of the weight we were carrying. The Colonel again led our company in the charge. You should have seen the look of terror on the Boers' faces when they saw our bayonets. Some would fire on us until we got about two yards from them and then they would throw down their arms and cry for mercy. Our Colonel was killed in the charge. The bu'lets were whizzing into the ground all around us: I don't think it will last much longer now as we have made a clean sweep of it. The Boers have cleared off towards Dun- dee. Our company lost very heavily in the charge. G,neral Buller said he could not find words enough to praise us. We marched through the streets of Lacy- smith on the 3rd March. It was a great thing. You will see pictures in the papers of us marching past the Town Hall. Sir Redvers Buller, Sir Charles Warren, Sir George White and all the chief officers were there. You might have heard of the troops in Ladysmith being in the best of spirits and good health, but I can tell you I never saw a poorer lot of soldiers in my life. They were starving on quarter rations and eating horsell,sh at that. The water here is the worst I have drunk."
The Treatment on Board Transports.

Mr. J. Meator, of Mersey-street. Warrington, has received the following letter from Private F. Martin, of the 2cul Battalioo Cheshire Regiment. It is dated Jacobsdal, Orange Free State, Sunday, February 25th, 1900 :—"I must say we had a very pleisant trip out to the Cape, but these troopships are 'thick.' It is 'shining' from a civilian's point of view to go down to Birkenhead or Liverpool to watch the progress of embarkation, &c, and to see the fine shipe,but, by way of a change, go to sea and realise for yourself as Thomas Henry Atkins the embarkations of troops, and it would make you wish you had never heard the word 'embark.' I noticed at Southampton whilst the troops inside the sheds on the docks were going through the preliminary tactics of stowing away a liner's cargo, the dock's gates were closed to the public, but as soon as this was practically I finished with Tommy was driven on buard,and from the iron sides of this monster boat was allowed to say adieu' to his friends who might have come some considerable distance to see him. Friends in this case may just as well find out the route the regiment is going to Southampton by and get on al railway bridge and shake a handkerchief at the first passing train. The life on a liner or transport is in one , word miserable—food bad, water ad sleeping accom-

modation awful, but I cannot give you details on so small a sheet of paper. The weather was bnutiful the whole way, bet we Cielfe ati pre:ty glad whrt we ran in Capetown harb4ur. We did the voyage in 20 days, landing a the night of the 27th, and entrai,ed for De Aar, toe base of operations. Toe people at Capetown seemed very loyal, afti,theerctl us f:oin every polnt. We have had a good bit of knocking about laeety, but not much fi4hting. We marcUed on this place and took it, after five hours fighting, but they seemed Co know the Cheshires were on the warpath. Jacobsdal is a pretty little place. W, have had some hard lines since the Boere captured a convoy of provisions, and we were on half rations for nearly two weeks, and during that time we were doing the heaviest work. The water was bad and scarce, and we had to march six or eight hours in topical heat without any water."

div.head: Trooper J. W. Broadbent with Kitchener.
div.p: Trooper J. W. Broadbent with Kitchener.

The following ere extracts from letters received by Mrs Broadbent, The Hollies, La•cnford, front her son, Trooper J W Broad'sent, who is serving with the 22nd Company (Cheshire) Imperial Yeoenany Matjesfontein (or Matjeskloof ?), March Btb. Just got here alter leaving Maitland Camp last night at 10 p.m. We are fairly comfortable, eight in a carriage. We hope to get to Naauwport to-morrow night:. We lift camp yesterday at two hours' nctice—a great rush, and there was a bit of a railway accident this morning ; we ran into a truck. We have all got our horses, and stop now and then to feed and water them. We don't get much rations served out, but get plenty of grapes. Sze., at stations. Just off.

Written in the train between Matjaskloaf and aIAIII w- poort, March 8:h. I sent you a hurried card frock, Matjesfontein where we stopped ta feed and water the horses and get some tea. There has been a bit of re- bellion at Yictoria West, and we are to be ready to turn out at 5.30 tc-morrow mornfng. I hope it won't be all over. We have just passed a train and hear that it is all ovcr, but I don't believe ic. We sa.v some priso ter in Capetown, I think they were goiw, to be pat on to the Lake Erie. This is a bleak drearyttuntry, but we are hiving a picnic. I weigh 93t. 121 b. in my shirt, heavier than ever before. VVa left in such a hurry I cauH not oring all I waned, but; have got m9at,lczeriges an 1 kola nut. Will write again for this mail.

De Aar, March lith, Sunday. We arrived here 6 pm. on Friday, we did not get out at Victoria West, as we thought we might have to, but sltpt in our puttees and were ready ta turn out at 5 a.m. I rather enjojed the journey than otherwise, it is a bleak country, hardly any cultivation ; nothing but leepj.:3 and a few ostrich farms. We slept in the train. Friday night,at least I was oo guard from 10 to 12 p.m. and 4 to 6 a.m. We ITlA:ched up laeresone mile, next morning, pitched our teats, &:. It is much colder at night and hotter in the day than it was at MaitlaGd. Toe first shot of the war was fir-d a few yards from this railway s-,stion an I there i 3 a em dl kopje two miles in front of our claw, the firs", the Boers were drivel from. Tnere art two gues on Ic)pjes near here' and picquets all relent!. It is a lar;;"e sandy plain with kopj, s all touud. 1 here are a lot of troops here.tbe Suffulks are here. I knew some of tne offieers in R sn- goon. We have been served out with helmets to-Jay. There are plenty of places to wash in and a small swimm'ng bath, 21t. deep, made of caevas. Our horses are all right, but were done up after the journey. A Boer spy came in our train and was taken prisoner ashes could not give an account of himself. Lord Kitehener was round our camp as soon as we got here. To-morrow we start at 3 p.m. with hirn, the Elamplaires, and some others to march 30 miles with two days' rations, to look up a lot of rebels. We are going in a while column. If we had gone to the front at Victoria West 15 scouts were to have gone out with Captain Danie:a ; I was going to be one. The latest report is that we—the 22nd Company—are to be Kitchener's escort. We start to-morrow anyhow. lam just finishing this off in the Soldiers' Home, a tent. We had a church service ad band this morning. lam feeling very fit ; we don't get much to eat here. I have talked to a Boer woundfd prisoner and have seen a lot of soldiers who have been wounded. Tile name of the place we are going to is Bridport (or Britstown). It is very interesting seeing, the soldiers writing letters, in some cases for one another. We are all very keen about to-morrow. WR are all a bearded,dirty looking lot now. These rebels want clear- ing out at once. The post box is just closing. I must stop Monday, March 12th. We are just saddling up to start in an hour, 3 p.m. We do 15 miles to-day, eleee out, then march into Bridport to-morrow. Rations, eight biscuits and one tin of meat for two days. Kitchener is our General. Dear love to all.—Josw.

div.head: Warrington Man's Trying Experiences. "Two Horses Shot Dead Under Him."
div.p: A Warrington Man's Trying Experiences. "Two Horses Shot Dead Under Him."

Mrs. Thud, 3, Providence-place, Warrington, has received an interesting letter from her husband, Private T. Dood, who is serving in the Free State with the 18th Regiment Cheshire Company of Mounted Infantry. It reads as follows :—" I write these few lines to you just to Ist you know that I am still alive and kicking. How I am living God only knows, I don't. I have been in three battles, and we have lost a great many men, but we beat their best army and captured their general (his name is Cronp) and 5,000 prisoners on the 28th ol Fotruary. I don't think the war will last much longer now. We are only two days march off Bioemfontien, the capital of the Orange Free State, and we start on Wednesday. I would like to see the latest papers ;we can't get anything here, and as for food we are starving to death. We have got no tents to get in out of the rain, and we have to sleep out in the rain every night. Our clothes are wet through till the sun dries them on our back. It is seven days since I was able to wash my face, and I have not had a shave since I left Aldershot, so you can tell what a beard I have got. You must not be alarmed when I tell you that I have had two horses shot dead under me and I have lost all my kit with my saddle. I have nothing in the world to stand up in only what lam wearing at the present time. It is five weeks since I washed my shirt and stockings ac I have not a change to put on. It is cruel men dying every minute in the day from wounds and rheumatic. I gave 33 for a drink of water the other day and 103 for a half ounce of tobacco and I was glad to get it I can tell you. . . . I hope the.day is not far off when we shall meet again in Old England. I expecc to be home by Walking Day at the latest now. I suppose you read about the relief of Kimberley and the capture of Cronje. lam very proud to tell you I was in the whole affair under Lord Roberts and we were thanked by the Queen, the Prince of Wales and Parliament. Don't forget to write as soon as you can and send a paper. I would like a bit of tobacco if you would send it. I hope I will have batter news next time.—From your loving husband and "a soldier and a man."

div.head: LATE PRIVATE MALKIN,
div.p: THE LATE PRIVATE MALKIN,
Memorial Service.

Oa Sunday, evening a service in memory of the late Private J. W. Malkin, of the Warrington Ambulance Cerps, whose death at Capetown was reported last week, was held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legh-street. The deceased, prior to leaving for the Cape, was a regu- lar attender at the chapel and Sunday school, and his death will be deeply regretted by all connected with the place of worship. There was a large congregation which included the deceased's relatives, Captain Waring an a number of members of the Ambulance Corps. The anthem" Vital spark,' was rendered by the choir, and the organist, Mr. F Podmore, played the Dead March in " Saul." _ _

The Rev. C. Firma was the preacher, and at the close of his discotirse feelingly alluded to the deceased's con- nection with the shape!. He said that for some years John W Malkin was a scholar in the Sunday school con- nected with that place of worship, and during the whole of the time he was with them he was regular in his at- tendance, and exemplary in his conduct. Tense who knew him best remembered him with pleasure, and spoke of him in terms of unqualified eulogy. While in the school he listened to expositions of Divine truth, and the lessons taught influenced him in after years. His connection with the local Ambulance Brigade was better known to some present than it was to himself (the preacher). He joined it, he was told, with the specific purpose of acquiring skill to render help and alleviate:pain A nobler purpose could not be conceived or a better way of accomplishing go3d,devised. Unselfish service for the good of others was practical Christianity. The unkeown writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews exhorted them to do good and communicate, and for their encouragement he infcrined them that with such sacrifiaes God was well pleased. Purejeligion and undefiled before God and the Father was to visit the widow and fatherless in their affliction and to keep themselves unspotted from the world. When the call came for Volunteers for the front he gave way to no unworthy fears, but placed his services at the dispcisal of his country and went. He left Warrington on ths 19:11 of December last never to see the old town aeain. On arriving at Capetown he was stationed at a hospital there, and they had no doubt be proved himself to be a careful, attentive and sympathetic nurse. White per- forming his duty he was attacked by enteric fever, and unfortunately succumbed to his powerful foe. Particu- lars had reached them about his last hours. No com • munications, perhaps, would ever be made to them about his spiritual condition. Let them hope that the truths he heard within those walls were for him the an- tidete of death. Seven hundred ambulance men had gone out to South Africa. John W. Malkin was one of the first to fall. Information of his death was obtained by his parents from one of the public prints, alai they could easily imagine the shock to their feelings which the painful intelligence produced. Captain Waring re- ceived a letter from headquarters in London in due clime, and then the parents received a letter from the Brigade Chief Superintendent, W. I. Church Brasier. The letter sent by Mr. Church Brasier did credit both to his head and his heart,and as it showed the esteem in which Malkin was held he could not refrain from quot- ing from it :—" We are proud of your son, as one who has lest his life in the service ofjhis country. He volun- teered for a work that has no glamour or glory about it, and in that work no lost his life. He came up here

div.head: MILITARY NOTES.
div.p: MILITARY NOTES.

Major Barroughs, late of the Swan Lancashire Regiment has been appointed to command the West kfrican Regiment and will have the rank of Lieut. Colonel. He joined the 2nd battalion South Lan- cashire Regiment in Oct 1870; was f,,r a time ad- jutant of the carpi; became Captain in 1881 and Major in 1889 retiring from the corps a short time ago when be joined the reserve of officers. Captain Prendergast, 2nd battalion South Lanca- shire • Regiment, has been appointed to the staff in India and has taken over the appointment of station staff officer at Roorkee.

Captain Bailey, Liver')3ol Regiment, who has of late been serving wi h the Depot Cpm-panies at Warrington has taken over the appointment of Adjutant of the 3rd battalion of the regiment now being form

Lieutenant Denhi, 2ad battalion, Liverpool Regiment. nom serving at Warringuon with the Depot Companies, will shortly be promoted to the rank of Captain in the regiment. Lieutenant Musgrave of the sth battalion Liver- pool Regiment with headquarters at Warrington has beem given a commission as Second Lieutenant in the Army S,2.rvice C)rps and will it is understood do duty at Aldershot. ,-econd Lieutenant Musgrave joined the battalion at Warrington in April 1895 and was promoted Lieutenant last December. Colonel Hare, late in command of the 2ad Batta- lion Cheshire Regiment, has taken over command of the 24Y,h (South Wales Borderers) Regimental district at Brecon Gil the transfer from the Com- mand of the 63rd (Aanche::tar) Regimental district, to which post he was appointed in March, 1898. Colonel Hare is well known locally as a former adjutant of the old 2nd Cheshire Militia. Colonel Roupell has been appointed to command the Royal Lancashire Reserve R'-qzinient, in which corps soldiers who have served in the South Lanca- shire Regiment a-e serving. Colon3l Roupell was formerly in command of the let Battalion East Surrey Regiment. Captain and Paymaster Harvest, who lately handed over his employment, in the station pay office at Warrington has assumed duty in South Africa.

div.head: WARRINGTON DISTRICT NURSING ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON DISTRICT NURSING ASSOCIATION.

At the quarterly meeting of the commit-me of the above ii.soai,tioh, held on Fri day last, toe following re- port was read : " Since toe last gen Tat c ,n3mittee meeting the pro- gre,s of the work has hat a severe cheek, owing to ill- ness among the nurses. When this began, in December there w,fe on the books 36 patens, several of whom were euff !ring from typhoid fever, oe other diseases re- quiring two visits daily, and a considerable expenditure of time at each visit. To lessen the strain on those who were able to be on duty during this time, steps had to be taken to curtail the work, and the doctors very considerately helpel by refraining from sending in any bat ureent cases, 93 that whereas ;ra November there were 40 now cases sent in, and 1296 visits paid. in Deceml;er there were 14 new case. sent in and 708 visits paid. A nurse was engaged to do temporary duty, but she only stayed 3 weeks, leaving to take a more congenial post on the staff of a Private Nursing some. January 1900 saw the work still under a cloud, there were 23 new cases and 709 visits paid. February found us gradually recovering from the effects of the sheck, with 37 new cases and 866 visits paid. All the nurses were again on duty and another one added to the staff. In March there were 34 new Cases, and the visits again reached the four figures, amounting to 1107. Expressions of appre- ciation from the patients are as frequent and hearty as ever, and the neglected state in which we find some of them makes us realize the sincerity of these expressions, and realize, too, the great need of such an association in Warrington. During the recent outbreak of Typhoid Fever in certain parts of the town the nurses found real work to do, and wry grateful for help and advice were the mothers who had several children ill at one time, or wives wha3e busbar.ds were ill. Sotnetim3a toe mother also was stricken down and had to watch her children suffer and even die, herself powerless to help them. To several cases of cancer dis- charged from the Infirmary and other Hospitals as incurable, the nurses h tve been able to minister, and if not to prolong life, at any rate to make the last weeks of pain and weakness a little more endurable than they otherwise would have been. S -nue, too, have been re- lieved to find that they could have the necessary atten- tion at home instead of being obliged to seek admission to the Workhouse liospit il, compelled not by poverty, but by the presence of some chronic disease or some injury whereby they are permanently disabled. In one ,or two instances, mothers of families who have become ' victims to the ravages of consumption, having no one to attend to them save their heedless little ones, or perhaps ' a kindly neighbour herself handicapped by the claims of a large family, have been, as they express it, "made over again " by the daily visits of a nuree,whe at least makes them clean and comfortable and keeps an oversight of the feeding. One old woman, living entirely alone, whom we had nursed before when she was incapacitated by a broken arm, Came under our care again, suffering from bronchitis, and so neglected was she that assuredly she must have died but for the services the nurse was able to render. Frequently has the nurse been a means of help and comfort to. those, who, unable to pay for assistance, were becoming. worn out by the long-con- tinued illness of their relatives. Bedsores have been pre- vented,and where they have been found to exist already by persevering and increasing care, have been much im- proved and in some oases completely healed. There has died since the last meeting, an old man who has been on the books almost since the b Tinning. We attended him in the first instance for a stubborn ulcer of the foot, but in course of time the other foot became gangrenous ' and so intense was the pain he suffered, so unsightly was the foot as it gradually decayed away, and so offensive I was the smell, that death came as a welcome releave to him and a relief to all whose duty it was to attend to him. During the 596 days he was our patient he was visited 848 tinsee. Of the 40 patients on the books March 31st, 7 have been on for more than 3 months. It is to chronic cases such as these usually deemed " uninterest- ing "that a nurse becomes almost indispensable.

div.p: PEN KETH.

TZB Ray. E. S. JACKSON.—Coramenting upon the re- moval of the Rev. E. S. Jackson, the "Wesleyan Metho- dist Church Record says :—" It is with very sincere regret that we notice Vie resignation and removal of the Rev. E. S. Jackson, M. A, Vicar of Sankey. For some years past his health has been failing, and of late he has felt himself quite upequal to his pulpit and pastoral duties. He is now taking final leave of his parishioners, after more than 20 years of scholarly and faithful ser- vice. It MIS be permitted to say that the Vicar he .4 ever shown himself broad-minded and large-h9arted,and has won the warm esteem of every Methodist in the parish. We fervently desire his speedy recovery,:and trust that in some more genial climate he may render many years of happy useful service to the cause of Christ."

div.head: Temperance Mission Lodge, 1.0.G.T.
div.p: Temperance Mission Lodge, 1.0.G.T.

The weekly session of the above lodge was held on Wednesday in the Mission Room, Academy-st., Bro Roberti,. CT., presided over a good attendance. One candidate was proposed for membership. Arrangements wen, made for a" Social" to be held on the 25th inst. A vote of sympathy was ordered to be sent to Bro Hall on the death of his wife. Bro Price then spoke a few words. The following programme was then rendered:—Bro Twigden, reci- tation," The Signboard," and song," Nay. John."; sister Nurse, recitation, " Foiring Butther," ; Bro O'Brien, song," Our ship is afloat,"; Sister Sheath, jun., recitation, "Down in the Mire,"; Bro C J Sheath, song, "Look not upon the wine,"; Bro J Sheath, recitation, "The Psalm of Life." Bro Littler- land male a few remarks on Lord Peel's minority report on the Royal Licensing Committee. Bro Nurse, song, "The Boys of the Old Brigade." The odge was closed in due form by Bro Roberts, C.T•

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.

A rneetine of Liberals was bele in the Town Hall; Ear!esteem, on Weeeesday evening. Mr Cr W Racehas. J.P , presidee, ieieperteil by Mr E J C Morton, M.P., fee, D -eenperre eltaers J Proet, B Harrison, R 0 Rawlins, J "ether. J Daereca. etre 11 B Shore, oreaniziug ageat for the Newton Division Liberal Association. Letters of apology were read from Dr Leathern (Ashton Polling Dis- trict) Rev F E Miller, Rev J H Riddette (Hayduck), Messre Halliday, Blaney, and Aitken (Penketh). The Chairman said the expediency of holding liberal meetines in the present circumstances in political affairs in many parts of the country was rather doubted, and people had been met with the charge that we had only got one thiag to talk about, and up et that one subject the Liberals were not united,eud had not made up their minds what they should think. It was quite true that the one eubject which monopolised the minds of most people at present was a very abs n•bing one, and it was equally true that the Liberal party were in the process of making up their minds about it. But it must not be forgotten that they were waiting for inforne.tion. Some day that information would be given to tnem,and until it was they were not fully able to make up their minds, and especially upon the pert of the subject of the way In which this war in South Africa was brought about. When they got information and could make up their mines they should do so rapidly and award the blame where they thought it was due. (Hear, hear.) The expediency of holding a meeting was con- sidered by the committee of the 300, and as they could get so sympathetic and so good a a speaker as Mr. Morton they decided they should not hesitete a moment about holding it. It was better they should meet and thrash out the engrossing subject which filled our mind s at the present time. The wee was consuming the best beoad of the nation and was taking up a great deal of the I money of the taxpayer and they were bound to consider theee points and to feel;a deep interest in it. There were o'her things in connection with it will Is deinended their attention. It hed brought out the unity of the Empire in a way which few of them would have theueht possible It had sheen to the world the solidarity of tee British Empire. It had made us proud that we were Englishmen end that we had such an empire. It was rue that Liberals were cot all agreed upei points in the war, but they were all agreed epee the bravery of our Ceionial awl British troops. (Hear, hear.) There was no course possiede but to go on and bring this war to a suceessful issue at speedily as possible. We hal sacrificed much and we should have to sacrifice more, but when the end was brought about we should feel we It ,d done our duty iu terminatine it. But because there was war in South Africa, thee die not forget thA they were Engiish Liberals, They did not forget that they had battles tn fieht at borne in conneetioa with home affairs, sal before very long there might Ice a general election in the country and they did not forget th It they in the Newton Division were strongly desirous of returning a Liberal candidate at the head of the poll. (Hear, hear.) They had fought many battles to try and win the Newton Division for a Liberal, but So far they had not succeeded, but if they_ stuck to it they would succeed. For the lent 12 months they had been working for that end, and Mr. Shores had been doing a great deal of work to promote what they hoped might be a victory when the time came. They were organising their forces in the polling districts in order to be reedy for the fray wnen it came. Theme were many national interests they had to look after for the well- being and prosperity of the men, women and children of this country. There was a Reuse of Lerde land taxation, temperance rerorm, and many other questions which they wanted Parliament to give its attention to , for a time in order that they might be brought to a satis- factory cenclesien. He concluded by moving" that this meeting of Newton Division Liberals is of tee opinion that a desirable crei setisfactere settlement of South Africa can only be found by bringing the war to a suc- cessful conclusion, and by subsequently eiving to all parts of South Africa the fullest measure of self govern- ment comottible with its future peace and prosperity. This tneeiiing urges the Liberal leaders to promote tho-e measures and reforms to which the Liberal party is pledged." Mr. „I H Profit seconded and said because President Kruger had solemnly appealed to the weighty arbitra- ment of war, he was now in the process of making his bed anl he must lie on it when the time came. He did not understand the position of thos ) gentlemen who opposed the war out of simple hatred Co Mr. Ceamber- lain. He did not look opan him as the author of the war. Ele, Mr. Profit, WAS no great admirer of Mr. , Chamberlin, but whatever his faults he was not res. pensible for the war, and as a Liberal he was pleased with many aspects of the struggle.. Our hest men were giving up their blood in the struggle.- We had heard a greet deal about a certain raid, but he Would like to ask the Boers if they had not heard of a certain raid also when P,etoriane went in the country of a neighbouring chief and in addition to other acts of violence seivd 17 children and carried them off as slaves to their own country. We ha d been a true brother to the Boer, we had assisted him when he was in bankruptcy, and when the Zulus might have eaten him up, we rescued him from their jaws. The Boers had flouted our flag, they had hindered and insulted our missionaries and had trodden down the poor natives and ha] wronged our on countrymen. He hoped when peace came it would be permanent and prosperous. (Applause.) Mr E J C Morton, M.P. supported the resolution. He said it was perhaps one of the worst features of the fact that we were at war, that that war obliterated and obscured from our minds all those measures of reform which they as Liberals wanted to see cars ied into law. That was an nntortunate incident aril sequence of any war, and he believed that there never lived a Liberal in the history of the woild who aid not hate war for its own sake. (Hear. hear.) He was glad to find that from the way in which they had received the speech of the seconder of the resolation that they recog- nised the fact that while we were in this war we were engaged in fighting out a quarre in which it could not be said with a distinctness and enthusiasm with which we sometimes beard the extreme Peace party say that this was unjust. Be bed , spent an enormous amount of trouble and time to get at the real fact about the rights and wrongs of the war,and he was bound to say that he had come to the conclusion that a more complicated issue he had never known dur- ing the 25 years he bad studied the politics of this coun- try. There bad been faults on both sides.and one of the gravest faults he felt inclined to charge Mr Chamberlain with was that he had put this country, by his reckless diplomacy, in a far worse position in the eyes of the world, that it was before. Tne contention of the Boers was preposterous. They might argue that the Boers were in the wrong, but wrong was not suffi lent to justify the war. 'That they were in the wrong he was quite clear of in his own mind, and the worst thing about it was that the reason they could not find anyone of Liberal sympathies who would not agree to that pro- position that the Boer contention was a preposterous one, Was because of the inept diplomacy with which Mr Chamberlain conducted our case. He believed it was a fact that the almost only reason that did make any Englishman sympathise with che Been was that they were a very small people, and we a big nation, and there was a very natural feel- ing to sympathise with the smaller people. But this fact was quite irrelevant to the question whether they were right or wrong. He was constantly being reminded of the fact that people would go straighter.and coral right in the conclusions they arrived at if they would pay an elementary regard to the four rules of arithmetic The area of the whole country south of the Zanzibar river, with the exception of a little strip on the West coast, which was under the dominion of Germany, and a strip on the East coast, under Portugal, was an area inhabited mainly by people of Dutch races or by pe-mle of British rac , and that area constituted the whole area dominated either by the British or the Dntch. The size of that area was almost the same as Great Ritain, Ireland, France, Italy and Germany together, and the population was only about the same as London. Think what that meant. There were about 5 millions of people, of whom al-nut 4 millions were black. It was not a case of land grabbing, it was a case of going into no man's land and reclaiming from the waste into civilisation certain land and leaving plenty of mons for the black population to roam about and till farms for themselves. The area of the Transvaal was almost the same as the area of Great Britain and Ireland together, and the population was less than a million white and black, the total white population being about 200,000, and among that the Boer Dutch population numbered only 80,000, and the white outlanders about 120,000. They could not say it was a case of people fighting for their own country against Great Britain who was trying to take it from them. They had a fragment °Patch living in that area and a fragment of British in a territory which belonged to neither, and the question was which of these two was to rule, and that was the issue. (Hear, hear.) Of the two sides we said the outlanders because they were in the majority. Some said the Boers because they were there first. -52 years ago there had never been a single white man in that area, Mr. Gladstone's great effort in the cause of peace after Mejuba Hill had militated against peace,and the re- suit was such that no other nation was likely to follow our experience. The Boers took it as a sign of weakness and the result was a spirit of jingoism on the part of the Boers. He trusted the war would be brought to a speedy conclusion. He knew it would make the living of the Dutch and British together a more difficult thing than it was before. He hoped the Liberal party would not split itself up in opinion so as to weaken it when its Voice had to be heard in the settlement. It was con- stantly being stated by the extreme Peace party among Liberals in this country that the war was a Capitalists war, got up by a lot of rich capitalists for their own personal interests. He was not going to deny that the Capitalists of the Rhodesian fac- tion had had a lot to do with the getting up of the War, and they had profited by it in the juggling of shares,and he had no sympathy with that gang, but he asked them to remember they were not the only people who pro- duced it. When the Boer Government took a census of the town of Johannesburg which was buiit entirely by Outlanders labour, money and energy, they in 1896 returned the population at 103,000. According to their papers the Official Boers who came in to

gaoern the town against the will of the pee-We. nurn`lerc. 5,001, !,,a,vi.ng 98,000 bona-fide ou.lAhd-rs :tti•A ne,rly 31tah Tnese men ha l 1n...,t3.,5ian capitalists, but they were afraid :13.4.t as a reiailt of the war, the settle- moot wimld ne andA ovei• to the Rhodesian party and they were most apprehensive of this, and were Tri.,4st anxious that we sh:ul-.1 tindtir.:Can.: that though th.iy had supported the war they did not want the whole thing put into the hen 'ls of Mr. Rhodes, and they wanted a man sending out there capable of resist- ing Mr. Knodes, and the man they hoped would be sent was Sir Cnaries Warren. (Rear, hear.) lie briefly touched on matters which :itiould engage the attention of the cAritry when tho war was over and said he looked forward to a future for this country of which we might well be punli, 11.1.1 he also begged them to remember that they as Liberals must feel that the strength of the empire ckpeadei ultimately not upon glorious ideas such as they heard from jingo speakers but upon the well being and eoucation af everyoue em its citiz-ms however humble lits stati,,n might be, that they might lay the true found ttioa for Pany greatmess in the firure. (Applause.) Votes of thanks ti the Speaker and Coalman termin- ated the meeting.

div.head: NEWTON-IN-MAKERFIELD DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTIONS.
div.p: NEWTON-IN-MAKERFIELD DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTIONS.
The Poll.

ai Monday Ihe contests for the Town Hall and Crow-lane Wards of the Newton-in-Makertield Urban District Council took place under very favour- able circumstances. The candidates were,tor Town Hall Ward : Mr George F Ciarire,and Mr W Gilmour and for Crow-lane Ward; Pr Latham, and Mr J Fitzgerald. The polling stations were at the Earlestown Dis- trict School for Town Hall Ward, two booths, with Mr W W Shirley, and NIA. G Strniger as presiding officers and at Wedeyau School, one booth for Crow- lane Ward, with Mr A Bowes as presiding officer. The polling opened precisely at 12 o'clock, but until after 1 o'clock very little was done, and be- t wean that hour and 2 o'clock the booths were fairly busy. Each co the candidates were fairly well sup- plied with conveyances for bringing up the voters, and numerous election posters were displayed on the sides of the vehicles, The electors were asked to vote" for Clarke and a constant water supply," " vote for Latham and batter sanitation," "vote for Fitzgerald the practical candidate." The voting was remarkably light in both wards, due no doabt to the fact that at the Viaduo; Works, overtime was being worked and many were thus unable to record their votes. Precisely at 8 o'clock p.)llieg ceased, and the votes were conveyed to the Town Hall to be counted, Jr. W. W. Shirley, acting as returnbag officer. la the room were the candidates and their agents, and Messrs W Coiling wool, W Beatty, and N Siddeley, councillors. The couating was pro- ceeded with expeditiously and at 840 the result was announce I to those in the roam, the crowd out- side anxiously awaiting the iiatelligence. Mr. Shirley announced that the result was as follows :

The result was variously received, and Mr. Gil- mour proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Shirley for the way in which he had conducted the election.

Mr. Firzgorald seconded, and Mr. Clarke and Dr. Le; ham supported. _gr. Shirley suitably acknow- ledged the vote. Tee figures were afterwards announced from the balcony of the Town Hall, and were received with cheers.

Mr. Gilmour stepped forward and addressing the crowd below said he thanked them most heartily for r-turning him that day, not only for the Town Hall Ward, but for the whole of the Newton-in- Makerfield district (a voice "3till at it again.") They knew he was labouring under great difficulties. They knew he WAS away on a sick bed, but he came to fight their battles and would do at all times and he thanked them for the trouble they had taken in voting for him. (Cheers.) Mr. J Fitzgerald saiduhe thanked them very much for the honour they had conferred on him that day, by returning him at the head of the poll, and he especially thanked all those who worked so heartily and sincerely for him. He could assure them that at all times he should consider it his duty to look after their interests. (Cheers.)

Dr. Latham thanked the 174 voters in Crow-lane Ward who that day recorded their votes in the cause of progress and efficiency. He should always be ready to place his services at the disposal of any party whatever may be its colour or creed providing that party had a desire to oust men who represented any interest which was opposed to the iaterest of the Township. Mr. G. F. Clarke, thankel all those who had seen their way torecord their votes in his favour, for the hearty support they had given him on that occasion. He was again in the position of being the defeated candidate, but he ventured to say that was not his last attempt, though his second fight but he hoped on the next occasion to ride home to victory. (A. voice: "You'll be a Parnellite next.") The interruption was not one that would carry any weight with him. He had lost considerably that day because he would not repudiate those opinions and convictions which he declared he held, and no Parnellite support would be studied by him for the sake of the men who recorded their votes in his favour. He stood for his honest convictions, and if he fell, he fell in making a good fight. And on any occasion when the interest of the ratepayers deman- ded it. and when any ward desired a canaidate, he should give it consideration, and take up their cause. He then called for cheers for Mr. Gilmour which were heartily given.

div.head: GRAPPEN HALL. A GRAPPENHALL LAMENT.
div.p: GRAPPEN HALL. A GRAPPENHALL LAMENT.

LOST, STOLEN OR STRAYED, an old and valued friend, well-known to every parishioner, and to thou- sands besides—one which for generations has faithfully served its purpese and done it without stint,or grudging. Time was back in the good old coaching days when steppages were regularly made in its vicinity, and when the high and low, the young and old were pleased to par- ticipate in its refreshing supplies who thought water of this kind without the addition of W . . . . quite good enough for them. The Guard invariably filled' a large jar, and took it with him so that others might sample the water which in those days had such a wonderful name for excellenee. Bit it has fallen upon evil days. It is reporeel that a high official of the Runcorn District Council I mean a tail gentleman, has had the water enalvsed. And the remarks on the analysis are. "1 cannot reconarnead this as a good water for domestic use." But a few others who are interested in the matter have also sent a sample of the water to be analysed. Not only do the figures in almost every instance show a decided improvement on the sample sent by the Coun- cil's official. But the remarks state "This is a high class water." Viet,at makes the matter inexplicable is that the two samples frcm the same pump were sent to the same analyst. Property owners here have been in- formed on the strength of the official's analysis that the pump water was condemned, and they must get their supply from the town main, which has during the past two or three months been taken to Mr. Dakin's tanyard. FOUND ! Yes it is in position again, brought back and replaced. Its removal was not of its own wish or choice, but it was ruthlessly torn away, and forcibly de- tained for two eltys much to the annoyance, and incon- venience of its regular visitors. But it looks strange. Y. It has been raised. The District Council seem rather in a raising mood lately ; but a week or two ago, and the salaries of their two surveyors were raised. The expense connected with the pump, though needless, will be small. But the salaries are raised by £3O each per annum and extras. But why the outlay on the Pump if it is condemned and why inform the public that such is the case if it is not so? The pump in question is known far and wide as supplying an excellent water, hundreds of tired, weary horses stop when they near it, asking their drivers in silent language to give them a drink, and appear pleased when their thirst has been satisfied. Cyclists quit the saddle when they approach it, and recognise that in it there is a friend to all and a foe to none. Yet according to report the water has been con- demned. The oldest inhabitant cannot remember an epidemic in the neighbourhood where the water is consumed. But we have had it, and even at the present time it exists in the locality in the form of diphtheria. If the Inspector would look into and remedy actual nuittees such as the emptying of closets some of Which have not been attended to for three or four years, and what may seem incredible at the present is the fact that some of the closets are within two or three yards eif the back doors se of the houses. There are great, and long standing nuisances in the parish. It may not be too muell to hope that now matters have begun to receive attention that a general investigation will take place and radical remedies be applied.—Yours.
NEMO.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. THE MARGARINE ACT 1887. AND THE SALE OF FOOD Re DRUGS ACT, 1899. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the Local Govern- ment Board have by General Order No. 40834, and dated the 28th February, 1900, directed the manner in which the Registration of Manufactories of Margarine or Margarine Cheese and the premises wherein the business of a wholesale dealer in Margarine or Margarine Cheese is carried on should be given effect to and which Order provides as follows : ARTICLE I.—This Order shall come into operation forthwith, and shall remain in force until We shall otherwite direct ; and the Order of 1887 is hereby re- scinded: Provided that in every case where a Manufactory of Margarine, or an owner or occupier carrying on the manufacture of Margarine has been duly registered,and such registration has effect at the date of this Order, such registration shall, notwithstanding the rescission of the Order of 1887 but subject to the provisions of Article W. of this Order, continue to have effect: Pro- vided also, that any book which prior to the date of this Order has been used by a local authority in pursu- ance of the Order of 1887 for purposes of registration shall, so far as such book contains any entry applicable to any such case as aforesaid, be deemed to be part of the register of the local authority for the purposes of this Order. ARTICLE ll.—Every owner or cecupier of a Manu- factory of and every wholesale dealer in Margarine or Margarine-cheese in England and Wales who shall make application to the proper local authority for a Certifi- cate of Registration under the Act of 1887 and the Act of 1899, or under either of the said Acts, shall, in his application, state the following particulars : (a.) The name and addrees of the owner or occupier or wholesale dealer making the application. (b.) The situaVon of the manufactory, or of the premises wherein the business of the wholesale dealer is carried on. (c.) The name and address, or names and addresses, of tbe owner or owners, or occupier or occupiers, or wholesale dealer or dealers, carrying on the manu- facture or the business. Every such application shall be signed by the person making the same, or by someone acting on his behalf. ARTICLE lII.—If the application is in due form, the local authority shall cause the Manufactory, or the Premises, as the case may be, to be registered by enter- ing in a book the particulars of the application for regis- tration; and thereupon a Certificate in the Form A. set forth in the Schedule hereto shall be issued by the local authority to the person applying for the same. ARTICLE IV.—Wh( re soy change occurs in the persons carryieg on the manufacture, or the business, written notice thereof shall be given by the owner or occupier of the Manufactory, or by the wholesale dealer carrying on the business, to the local authority, and the Register shall thereupon be amended by making therein the requisite alteration, and an endorsement shall be made by the local Authority on the Certificate in 'accordance with the Form B, set forth in the said Schedule. The Local Authority for the Administrative County of Chester, excluding the municipal Boroughr of Conglpton Hyde, Macclesfield, and Stalybridge, is the Cheshire County Council, and all aprlications for the Registra- tion of Manufactories of Margarine or Margarine Cheese, or any premises wherein the lewdness of a wholesale dealer in Margarine or Margarine Cheese is carried on must be made to the undersigned, the Clerk to such Local Authority, when if such application is in order a Certificate of such Registration in the form prescribed by the foregoing Order will be forwarded to the person applying for the same. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. th March 1900.
